﴿And Allah sends down from the sky water﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and He revives the earth after its death﴾, after its barrenness and its being worn out. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen﴾, with the hearing of the hearts and not the hearing of the ears.

﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾, an admonition. ﴿We give you to drink﴾.

The people of Medina, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and 'Asim read ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ﴾ with a fatha on the nun (nasqikum).

The rest read it with a damma on the nun (nusqikum), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, saying: "Because it is a drink that is continuous."

It is related from al-Kisa'i that the Arabs say أسقيته نهرا (asqaytuhu nahran, "I gave him a river to water him") and أسقيته لبنا (asqaytuhu laban, "I gave him milk") when they mean to provide a continuous supply, but when they mean that they gave him a single drink, they say سقيناه (saqaynahu), without the alif.

Others said: "They are two dialects, and what indicates this is the saying of Labid in describing the watering:

"He gave drink to my people, the Banu Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilal."

He combined the two dialects.

﴿مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "from what is in their bellies", and he did not say بطونها (butuniha), although الأنعام (al-an'am, the livestock) is a plural. Al-Mubarrad said: the pronoun refers to النعم (al-ni'am, "the cattle"), and النعم and الأنعام are one and the same, and the word النعم is used. He cited in evidence a rajaz verse of one of the Bedouin:

"When you see the stars of Leo
Rise over its forehead and the khara and the kanad,
And Suhayl sets at al-Fadih, and it becomes spoiled,
And the milk of the she-camels becomes good and cool."

He did not say فبردت (fabaradat), because he referred it back to اللبن (al-laban, "the milk") or الخراة (al-kharah). [Thus in the original.]

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: نعم (ni'am, "cattle") is masculine and feminine. Whoever makes it feminine does so for the sense of plurality, and whoever makes it masculine does so for the form of the word, and because it has no singular from its own form.

A poet said about it:

"Every year there are cattle that you keep,
A people impregnate them and you deliver them,
Indeed they have palm trees, so they do not protect them."

Al-Kisa'i said: the pronoun refers back to what is intended, in the bellies of what has been mentioned.

Some of them said: he meant the bellies of this thing, like Allah's saying: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord"﴾, and His saying: ﴿"And indeed I am sending a gift to them"﴾ up to ﴿So when he came to Solomon﴾, and He did not say "she came."

Al-Salt al-'Abdi said:

"Indeed, generosity and manliness have enclosed
A grave in Marw, on the clear road."

Another said:

"And 'Afra' is the nearest of people to me in affection,
And 'Afra' is far from me, the one who turns away and holds back."

Another said:

"When people are people and the lands are in prosperity,
And the mother of 'Ammar is a friend who helps."

All of that is according to the meaning of this person and this thing.

Al-Mu'arrij said: the pronoun refers back to the part and the portion, as if He said: ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "We give you to drink from what is in their bellies," which is the milk, since not all of them have milk, but only those that have milk are watered, so the milk is implied in it.

﴿مِنْ بَيْنِ فَرْثٍ﴾, "from between dung", which is what is in the paunch; when it leaves it, it is no longer called فرث (farth). ﴿وَدَمٍ﴾, "and blood", ﴿لَبَنًا خَالِصًا﴾, "pure milk", purified from the dung and the blood and not mixed with them, ﴿سَائِغًا لِلشَّارِبِينَ﴾, "palatable to the drinkers", ready, pleasant, sliding down the throat without choking its drinker. It was said: no one has ever choked on milk.

Ibn 'Abbas said: when the animal eats the fodder and it settles in its paunch at that time, its lowest part is dung, its middle is milk, and its uppermost part is the blood of the liver. [So what was] of these three kinds is divided: the blood flows in the veins, the milk flows into the udder, and the dung remains as it is.

﴿وَمِنْ ثَمَرَاتِ النَّخِيلِ وَالْأَعْنَابِ﴾, meaning: this too is a lesson, in what We give you to drink and provide you with, from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes, ﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنْهُ﴾, "you take from it". The pronoun in His saying ﴿مِنْهُ﴾ refers back to those mentioned.

﴿سَكَرًا وَرِزْقًا حَسَنًا﴾, "intoxicant and good provision".

Some people said: al-sakar is wine, and al-rizq al-hasan is vinegar, grapes, dates and raisins. They said: this is the view on the prohibition of wine, and this view was held by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Amr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ayyub, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla and al-Kalbi. It is the narration of 'Amr ibn Sufyan al-Basri from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-sakar is what is forbidden of its fruit, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is lawful of its fruit.

As for al-sakar, it is the intoxicants of these foreigners, and as for al-rizq al-hasan, it is what you soak, what you make vinegar from, and what you eat.

He said: this verse was revealed when wine had not yet been forbidden, and its prohibition was revealed after that in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Al-Sha'bi said: al-sakar is what is drunk, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is eaten.

Al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas that the Abyssinians call vinegar al-sakar.

Others said: al-sakar is intoxicating nabidh, which is the steeped infusion of dates and raisins when it has fermented, and the boiled-down juice. This is the view of al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi, according to the narration of Mujalid, and Abu Rawq, and the view of al-Nakha'i, and the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: it is date nabidh.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Wine is what is made from grapes, sakar is from dates, bit' is from honey, mizr is from maize, [and al-bira] [as in the manuscript, though it is not found in the source] from wheat, and I forbid you from every intoxicant." [6] [Musnad Abi Ya'la, 13/216, with variation.]

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-sakar means taste; it is said: "This is sakar for you," meaning a taste for you.

He recited:

"I made the faults of the noble ones a taste."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾, "Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason."

﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ﴾, "And your Lord inspired the bee." That is, He cast [into its ears] or threw into its souls, and it understood it. The nahl (bee) is the wasps of honey, and its singular is nahlah.

﴿أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ﴾, "that take for yourselves houses in the mountains, in the trees, and in what they build". Ibn Zayd said: it means the vineyard.

﴿ثُمَّ كُلِي مِنْ كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ﴾, "Then eat from all the fruits". The meaning of "all" is not generality; it is like His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾, and His saying: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾.

﴿فَاسْلُكِي سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًا﴾, "So follow the ways of your Lord, submissively." That is, enter the paths of your Lord.

Some said: al-dhulul means the paths, and it is said they are made easy for the bees. Mujahid said: "No place is difficult for them that they have traveled."

Others said: al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees [in Tafsir al-Tabari (14/184): it is an attribute of the paths, attributed to Mujahid, then he mentioned the view that al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees, and he preferred the first].

Qatadah and others said: it means obedient and submissive.

﴿يَخْرُجُ مِنْ بُطُونِهَا شَرَابٌ مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ﴾, "From their bellies comes a drink of varying colours", white, red and yellow, ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾, "in it is healing for mankind."

It is related that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My brother has a pain in his stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." He went and came back and said: "I gave him to drink, and it did not help him at all." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Go and give him honey to drink, for Allah has spoken the truth and his brother's stomach has lied." [7] [Sahih Muslim, 7/26, and Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3/276.] So he gave him to drink, and it was as if he had been released from a fetter. [It was related by] 'Atiyyah from Abu al-Mutawakkil from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Mujahid said: ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ means in the Qur'an. The first view is more correct and better suited to the apparent sense of the Book.

Waki' related from Sufyan from Abu Ishaq from Abu al-Ahwas from 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), who said: honey is a healing from every disease, and the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts.

Al-A'mash from Khaytham from al-Aswad said: 'Abd Allah said: "Keep to the two healings: honey and the Qur'an."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾, that is, in what we have mentioned, ﴿لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾, "a sign for a people who reflect", so that they may take lesson.

﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ ثُمَّ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ﴾, "And Allah created you, then He takes you back", as children, youths and elders. ﴿وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرَدُّ إِلَى أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ﴾, "And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age", that is, its worst. It is said from this: "the man became base and despicable (dhall al-rajul wa-fasal, yarthul rudhalah wa-rudhulah, wa-radhalthuhu ana)" [Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/186].

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means to the lowest of life.

Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: it means senility.

Qatadah said: the most abject age is seventy years.

Al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: the most abject age is seventy-five years.

﴿لِكَيْ لَا يَعْلَمَ بَعْدَ عِلْمٍ شَيْئًا﴾, "so that he knows nothing after knowing", that is, he does not reason after his first reason at all.

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ قَدِيرٌ﴾, "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful." Its parallel is in Surat al-Hajj [Surat al-Hajj: 5].

﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ فِي الرِّزْقِ﴾, "And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. So those who have been favoured in provision will not give their provision ﴿عَلَى مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ﴾, "to what their right hands possess", of the slaves, so that they and their slaves would be equal in that." Allah, may His praise be exalted, says: they do not accept that they and their slaves be equal in what We have provided them, yet they have made My servants partners in My dominion and My authority. This parable is used to establish the proof against the polytheists. This is a parable which Allah, mighty and majestic, has coined: none of you shares his slave's wife, his relatives or his wealth with him. Will you then equate with Allah His creation and His servants? If you do not accept this for yourselves, then Allah is more worthy to be exalted above it, and do not equate any of His servants or creatures with Him [see Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/188].

'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: this verse was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran when they said: "Jesus is the son of God." It says: the master does not give back from what his right hand possesses from what He has provided, until the master and the owned are equal in the means of livelihood. How then do you accept for Me what you do not accept for yourselves? Its parallel is in Surat al-Rum: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [Surat al-Rum: 28] [a parable you witness].

He said: ﴿أَفَبِنِعْمَةِ اللَّهِ يَجْحَدُونَ﴾, "Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?" by associating others with Him.

'Asim read with the ta' (tajhadun, in the second person), because of His saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ﴾ and ﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ﴾.

The rest read with the ya' (yajhadun, in the third person), because of His saying: ﴿فَهُمْ فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ﴾ [Surat al-Nahl: 71], and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because the reported party is closer to it.

﴿وَاللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا﴾, "And Allah made for you spouses from yourselves", meaning that He created from Adam his wife Hawwa'. ﴿وَجَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَزْوَاجِكُمْ بَنِينَ وَحَفَدَةً﴾, "and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren."

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Ad'ha said: the hafadah are the in-laws, the husband's sons-in-law (who are married to his daughters).

Shu'bah related from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, who said: I heard Zirr ibn Hubaysh, a foreigner who had lived through the Jahiliyyah, say: "I used to hold the Mushaf for 'Abd Allah, and he came to this verse, and he asked: 'Do you know what al-hafadah are?' I said: 'They are a man's entourage.' 'Abd Allah said: 'No, but they are the in-laws.'" This is also the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: they are the servants.

Mujahid and Abu Malik al-Ansari said: they are the helpers. This is the narration of Abu Hamzah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Whoever helps you is your hafad."

A poet said:

"The young servants surround them, and they hand over
With their hands the reins of the camels."

'Ata' said: they are the man's children who help him, serve him, support him and attend to him.

Qatadah said: they are the servants, the ones who serve you among your children.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the banun (sons) are the young ones, and the hafadah are the older children who help him in his work.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the children's children.

Ibn Zayd said: they are the sons of the wife from her first husband. This is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the sons of a man's first wife.

Al-'Utbi said: the origin of hafd is racing toward danger and hastening in walking.

So it is said of everyone who hastens in service and work: hafadah, its singular being hafid. From this comes the supplication of the witr prayer: "To You we strive and hasten," meaning we hasten to work in Your obedience.

Ibn Jarir recited [for al-Ra'i]:

"I burdened with its unknown things Yamani she-camels
When the drivers hasten on their backs."

﴿وَرَزَقَكُمْ مِنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ﴾, "and provided you with good things. ﴿أَفَبِالْبَاطِلِ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾", "Then do they believe in falsehood?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: in idols.

﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, that is, the false monotheism; the devil commanded them to slaughter the baheerah, the saa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham. ﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ﴾, by what Allah made lawful for them, ﴿هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, they deny, they reject its being made lawful.

﴿وَيَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَمْلِكُ لَهُمْ رِزْقًا مِنَ السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾, that is, the rain, ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾, that is, the plants.

﴿شَيْئًا﴾. Al-Akhfash said: it is a substitute for rizq, and it has the meaning: they do not own any provision, a little or a lot. Al-Farra' said: shay'an (anything) is in the accusative because the word rizq is applied to it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [Surat al-Mursalat: 25-26], meaning it gathers the living and the dead. Similarly His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan near of kin﴾ [Surat al-Balad: 14-15].

﴿وَلَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ﴾, "and they are not able", that is, they have no power over anything. ﴿فَلَا تَضْرِبُوا لِلَّهِ الْأَمْثَالَ﴾, "So do not coin parables for Allah", that is, similitudes and likenesses, lest they liken Him to His creation and make a partner for Him, for He is One with no like. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ﴾, "Indeed Allah knows" the error of what they coin of parables for Him, ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, "and you do not know" the correctness of that from its error.

﴿And Allah sends down from the sky water﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and He revives the earth after its death﴾, after its barrenness and its being worn out. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen﴾, with the hearing of the hearts and not the hearing of the ears.

﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾, an admonition. ﴿We give you to drink﴾.

The people of Medina, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and 'Asim read ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ﴾ with a fatha on the nun (nasqikum).

The rest read it with a damma on the nun (nusqikum), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, saying: "Because it is a drink that is continuous."

It is related from al-Kisa'i that the Arabs say أسقيته نهرا (asqaytuhu nahran, "I gave him a river to water him") and أسقيته لبنا (asqaytuhu laban, "I gave him milk") when they mean to provide a continuous supply, but when they mean that they gave him a single drink, they say سقيناه (saqaynahu), without the alif.

Others said: "They are two dialects, and what indicates this is the saying of Labid in describing the watering:

"He gave drink to my people, the Banu Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilal."

He combined the two dialects.

﴿مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "from what is in their bellies", and he did not say بطونها (butuniha), although الأنعام (al-an'am, the livestock) is a plural. Al-Mubarrad said: the pronoun refers to النعم (al-ni'am, "the cattle"), and النعم and الأنعام are one and the same, and the word النعم is used. He cited in evidence a rajaz verse of one of the Bedouin:

"When you see the stars of Leo
Rise over its forehead and the khara and the kanad,
And Suhayl sets at al-Fadih, and it becomes spoiled,
And the milk of the she-camels becomes good and cool."

He did not say فبردت (fabaradat), because he referred it back to اللبن (al-laban, "the milk") or الخراة (al-kharah). [Thus in the original.]

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: نعم (ni'am, "cattle") is masculine and feminine. Whoever makes it feminine does so for the sense of plurality, and whoever makes it masculine does so for the form of the word, and because it has no singular from its own form.

A poet said about it:

"Every year there are cattle that you keep,
A people impregnate them and you deliver them,
Indeed they have palm trees, so they do not protect them."

Al-Kisa'i said: the pronoun refers back to what is intended, in the bellies of what has been mentioned.

Some of them said: he meant the bellies of this thing, like Allah's saying: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord"﴾, and His saying: ﴿"And indeed I am sending a gift to them"﴾ up to ﴿So when he came to Solomon﴾, and He did not say "she came."

Al-Salt al-'Abdi said:

"Indeed, generosity and manliness have enclosed
A grave in Marw, on the clear road."

Another said:

"And 'Afra' is the nearest of people to me in affection,
And 'Afra' is far from me, the one who turns away and holds back."

Another said:

"When people are people and the lands are in prosperity,
And the mother of 'Ammar is a friend who helps."

All of that is according to the meaning of this person and this thing.

Al-Mu'arrij said: the pronoun refers back to the part and the portion, as if He said: ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "We give you to drink from what is in their bellies," which is the milk, since not all of them have milk, but only those that have milk are watered, so the milk is implied in it.

﴿مِنْ بَيْنِ فَرْثٍ﴾, "from between dung", which is what is in the paunch; when it leaves it, it is no longer called فرث (farth). ﴿وَدَمٍ﴾, "and blood", ﴿لَبَنًا خَالِصًا﴾, "pure milk", purified from the dung and the blood and not mixed with them, ﴿سَائِغًا لِلشَّارِبِينَ﴾, "palatable to the drinkers", ready, pleasant, sliding down the throat without choking its drinker. It was said: no one has ever choked on milk.

Ibn 'Abbas said: when the animal eats the fodder and it settles in its paunch at that time, its lowest part is dung, its middle is milk, and its uppermost part is the blood of the liver. [So what was] of these three kinds is divided: the blood flows in the veins, the milk flows into the udder, and the dung remains as it is.

﴿وَمِنْ ثَمَرَاتِ النَّخِيلِ وَالْأَعْنَابِ﴾, meaning: this too is a lesson, in what We give you to drink and provide you with, from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes, ﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنْهُ﴾, "you take from it". The pronoun in His saying ﴿مِنْهُ﴾ refers back to those mentioned.

﴿سَكَرًا وَرِزْقًا حَسَنًا﴾, "intoxicant and good provision".

Some people said: al-sakar is wine, and al-rizq al-hasan is vinegar, grapes, dates and raisins. They said: this is the view on the prohibition of wine, and this view was held by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Amr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ayyub, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla and al-Kalbi. It is the narration of 'Amr ibn Sufyan al-Basri from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-sakar is what is forbidden of its fruit, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is lawful of its fruit.

As for al-sakar, it is the intoxicants of these foreigners, and as for al-rizq al-hasan, it is what you soak, what you make vinegar from, and what you eat.

He said: this verse was revealed when wine had not yet been forbidden, and its prohibition was revealed after that in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Al-Sha'bi said: al-sakar is what is drunk, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is eaten.

Al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas that the Abyssinians call vinegar al-sakar.

Others said: al-sakar is intoxicating nabidh, which is the steeped infusion of dates and raisins when it has fermented, and the boiled-down juice. This is the view of al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi, according to the narration of Mujalid, and Abu Rawq, and the view of al-Nakha'i, and the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: it is date nabidh.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Wine is what is made from grapes, sakar is from dates, bit' is from honey, mizr is from maize, [and al-bira] [as in the manuscript, though it is not found in the source] from wheat, and I forbid you from every intoxicant." [6] [Musnad Abi Ya'la, 13/216, with variation.]

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-sakar means taste; it is said: "This is sakar for you," meaning a taste for you.

He recited:

"I made the faults of the noble ones a taste."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾, "Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason."

﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ﴾, "And your Lord inspired the bee." That is, He cast [into its ears] or threw into its souls, and it understood it. The nahl (bee) is the wasps of honey, and its singular is nahlah.

﴿أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ﴾, "that take for yourselves houses in the mountains, in the trees, and in what they build". Ibn Zayd said: it means the vineyard.

﴿ثُمَّ كُلِي مِنْ كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ﴾, "Then eat from all the fruits". The meaning of "all" is not generality; it is like His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾, and His saying: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾.

﴿فَاسْلُكِي سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًا﴾, "So follow the ways of your Lord, submissively." That is, enter the paths of your Lord.

Some said: al-dhulul means the paths, and it is said they are made easy for the bees. Mujahid said: "No place is difficult for them that they have traveled."

Others said: al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees [in Tafsir al-Tabari (14/184): it is an attribute of the paths, attributed to Mujahid, then he mentioned the view that al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees, and he preferred the first].

Qatadah and others said: it means obedient and submissive.

﴿يَخْرُجُ مِنْ بُطُونِهَا شَرَابٌ مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ﴾, "From their bellies comes a drink of varying colours", white, red and yellow, ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾, "in it is healing for mankind."

It is related that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My brother has a pain in his stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." He went and came back and said: "I gave him to drink, and it did not help him at all." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Go and give him honey to drink, for Allah has spoken the truth and his brother's stomach has lied." [7] [Sahih Muslim, 7/26, and Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3/276.] So he gave him to drink, and it was as if he had been released from a fetter. [It was related by] 'Atiyyah from Abu al-Mutawakkil from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Mujahid said: ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ means in the Qur'an. The first view is more correct and better suited to the apparent sense of the Book.

Waki' related from Sufyan from Abu Ishaq from Abu al-Ahwas from 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), who said: honey is a healing from every disease, and the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts.

Al-A'mash from Khaytham from al-Aswad said: 'Abd Allah said: "Keep to the two healings: honey and the Qur'an."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾, that is, in what we have mentioned, ﴿لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾, "a sign for a people who reflect", so that they may take lesson.

﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ ثُمَّ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ﴾, "And Allah created you, then He takes you back", as children, youths and elders. ﴿وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرَدُّ إِلَى أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ﴾, "And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age", that is, its worst. It is said from this: "the man became base and despicable (dhall al-rajul wa-fasal, yarthul rudhalah wa-rudhulah, wa-radhalthuhu ana)" [Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/186].

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means to the lowest of life.

Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: it means senility.

Qatadah said: the most abject age is seventy years.

Al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: the most abject age is seventy-five years.

Ibn 'Abbas said: in idols.

﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, that is, the false monotheism; the devil commanded them to slaughter the baheerah, the saa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham. ﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ﴾, by what Allah made lawful for them, ﴿هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, they deny, they reject its being made lawful.

﴿وَيَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَمْلِكُ لَهُمْ رِزْقًا مِنَ السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾, that is, the rain, ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾, that is, the plants.

﴿شَيْئًا﴾. Al-Akhfash said: it is a substitute for rizq, and it has the meaning: they do not own any provision, a little or a lot. Al-Farra' said: shay'an (anything) is in the accusative because the word rizq is applied to it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [Surat al-Mursalat: 25-26], meaning it gathers the living and the dead. Similarly His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan near of kin﴾ [Surat al-Balad: 14-15].

﴿وَلَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ﴾, "and they are not able", that is, they have no power over anything. ﴿فَلَا تَضْرِبُوا لِلَّهِ الْأَمْثَالَ﴾, "So do not coin parables for Allah", that is, similitudes and likenesses, lest they liken Him to His creation and make a partner for Him, for He is One with no like. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ﴾, "Indeed Allah knows" the error of what they coin of parables for Him, ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, "and you do not know" the correctness of that from its error.

﴿And Allah sends down from the sky water﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and He revives the earth after its death﴾, after its barrenness and its being worn out. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen﴾, with the hearing of the hearts and not the hearing of the ears.

﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾, an admonition. ﴿We give you to drink﴾.

The people of Medina, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and 'Asim read ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ﴾ with a fatha on the nun (nasqikum).

The rest read it with a damma on the nun (nusqikum), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, saying: "Because it is a drink that is continuous."

It is related from al-Kisa'i that the Arabs say أسقيته نهرا (asqaytuhu nahran, "I gave him a river to water him") and أسقيته لبنا (asqaytuhu laban, "I gave him milk") when they mean to provide a continuous supply, but when they mean that they gave him a single drink, they say سقيناه (saqaynahu), without the alif.

Others said: "They are two dialects, and what indicates this is the saying of Labid in describing the watering:

"He gave drink to my people, the Banu Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilal."

He combined the two dialects.

﴿مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "from what is in their bellies", and he did not say بطونها (butuniha), although الأنعام (al-an'am, the livestock) is a plural. Al-Mubarrad said: the pronoun refers to النعم (al-ni'am, "the cattle"), and النعم and الأنعام are one and the same, and the word النعم is used. He cited in evidence a rajaz verse of one of the Bedouin:

"When you see the stars of Leo
Rise over its forehead and the khara and the kanad,
And Suhayl sets at al-Fadih, and it becomes spoiled,
And the milk of the she-camels becomes good and cool."

He did not say فبردت (fabaradat), because he referred it back to اللبن (al-laban, "the milk") or الخراة (al-kharah). [Thus in the original.]

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: نعم (ni'am, "cattle") is masculine and feminine. Whoever makes it feminine does so for the sense of plurality, and whoever makes it masculine does so for the form of the word, and because it has no singular from its own form.

A poet said about it:

"Every year there are cattle that you keep,
A people impregnate them and you deliver them,
Indeed they have palm trees, so they do not protect them."

Al-Kisa'i said: the pronoun refers back to what is intended, in the bellies of what has been mentioned.

Some of them said: he meant the bellies of this thing, like Allah's saying: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord"﴾, and His saying: ﴿"And indeed I am sending a gift to them"﴾ up to ﴿So when he came to Solomon﴾, and He did not say "she came."

Al-Salt al-'Abdi said:

"Indeed, generosity and manliness have enclosed
A grave in Marw, on the clear road."

Another said:

"And 'Afra' is the nearest of people to me in affection,
And 'Afra' is far from me, the one who turns away and holds back."

Another said:

"When people are people and the lands are in prosperity,
And the mother of 'Ammar is a friend who helps."

All of that is according to the meaning of this person and this thing.

Al-Mu'arrij said: the pronoun refers back to the part and the portion, as if He said: ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "We give you to drink from what is in their bellies," which is the milk, since not all of them have milk, but only those that have milk are watered, so the milk is implied in it.

﴿مِنْ بَيْنِ فَرْثٍ﴾, "from between dung", which is what is in the paunch; when it leaves it, it is no longer called فرث (farth). ﴿وَدَمٍ﴾, "and blood", ﴿لَبَنًا خَالِصًا﴾, "pure milk", purified from the dung and the blood and not mixed with them, ﴿سَائِغًا لِلشَّارِبِينَ﴾, "palatable to the drinkers", ready, pleasant, sliding down the throat without choking its drinker. It was said: no one has ever choked on milk.

Ibn 'Abbas said: when the animal eats the fodder and it settles in its paunch at that time, its lowest part is dung, its middle is milk, and its uppermost part is the blood of the liver. [So what was] of these three kinds is divided: the blood flows in the veins, the milk flows into the udder, and the dung remains as it is.

﴿وَمِنْ ثَمَرَاتِ النَّخِيلِ وَالْأَعْنَابِ﴾, meaning: this too is a lesson, in what We give you to drink and provide you with, from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes, ﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنْهُ﴾, "you take from it". The pronoun in His saying ﴿مِنْهُ﴾ refers back to those mentioned.

﴿سَكَرًا وَرِزْقًا حَسَنًا﴾, "intoxicant and good provision".

Some people said: al-sakar is wine, and al-rizq al-hasan is vinegar, grapes, dates and raisins. They said: this is the view on the prohibition of wine, and this view was held by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Amr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ayyub, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla and al-Kalbi. It is the narration of 'Amr ibn Sufyan al-Basri from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-sakar is what is forbidden of its fruit, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is lawful of its fruit.

As for al-sakar, it is the intoxicants of these foreigners, and as for al-rizq al-hasan, it is what you soak, what you make vinegar from, and what you eat.

He said: this verse was revealed when wine had not yet been forbidden, and its prohibition was revealed after that in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Al-Sha'bi said: al-sakar is what is drunk, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is eaten.

Al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas that the Abyssinians call vinegar al-sakar.

Others said: al-sakar is intoxicating nabidh, which is the steeped infusion of dates and raisins when it has fermented, and the boiled-down juice. This is the view of al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi, according to the narration of Mujalid, and Abu Rawq, and the view of al-Nakha'i, and the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: it is date nabidh.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Wine is what is made from grapes, sakar is from dates, bit' is from honey, mizr is from maize, [and al-bira] [as in the manuscript, though it is not found in the source] from wheat, and I forbid you from every intoxicant." [6] [Musnad Abi Ya'la, 13/216, with variation.]

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-sakar means taste; it is said: "This is sakar for you," meaning a taste for you.

He recited:

"I made the faults of the noble ones a taste."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾, "Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason."

﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ﴾, "And your Lord inspired the bee." That is, He cast [into its ears] or threw into its souls, and it understood it. The nahl (bee) is the wasps of honey, and its singular is nahlah.

﴿أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ﴾, "that take for yourselves houses in the mountains, in the trees, and in what they build". Ibn Zayd said: it means the vineyard.

﴿ثُمَّ كُلِي مِنْ كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ﴾, "Then eat from all the fruits". The meaning of "all" is not generality; it is like His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾, and His saying: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾.

﴿فَاسْلُكِي سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًا﴾, "So follow the ways of your Lord, submissively." That is, enter the paths of your Lord.

Some said: al-dhulul means the paths, and it is said they are made easy for the bees. Mujahid said: "No place is difficult for them that they have traveled."

Others said: al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees [in Tafsir al-Tabari (14/184): it is an attribute of the paths, attributed to Mujahid, then he mentioned the view that al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees, and he preferred the first].

Qatadah and others said: it means obedient and submissive.

﴿يَخْرُجُ مِنْ بُطُونِهَا شَرَابٌ مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ﴾, "From their bellies comes a drink of varying colours", white, red and yellow, ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾, "in it is healing for mankind."

It is related that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My brother has a pain in his stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." He went and came back and said: "I gave him to drink, and it did not help him at all." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Go and give him honey to drink, for Allah has spoken the truth and his brother's stomach has lied." [7] [Sahih Muslim, 7/26, and Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3/276.] So he gave him to drink, and it was as if he had been released from a fetter. [It was related by] 'Atiyyah from Abu al-Mutawakkil from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Mujahid said: ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ means in the Qur'an. The first view is more correct and better suited to the apparent sense of the Book.

Waki' related from Sufyan from Abu Ishaq from Abu al-Ahwas from 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), who said: honey is a healing from every disease, and the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts.

Al-A'mash from Khaytham from al-Aswad said: 'Abd Allah said: "Keep to the two healings: honey and the Qur'an."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾, that is, in what we have mentioned, ﴿لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾, "a sign for a people who reflect", so that they may take lesson.

﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ ثُمَّ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ﴾, "And Allah created you, then He takes you back", as children, youths and elders. ﴿وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرَدُّ إِلَى أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ﴾, "And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age", that is, its worst. It is said from this: "the man became base and despicable (dhall al-rajul wa-fasal, yarthul rudhalah wa-rudhulah, wa-radhalthuhu ana)" [Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/186].

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means to the lowest of life.

Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: it means senility.

Qatadah said: the most abject age is seventy years.

Al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: the most abject age is seventy-five years.

﴿لِكَيْ لَا يَعْلَمَ بَعْدَ عِلْمٍ شَيْئًا﴾, "so that he knows nothing after knowing", that is, he does not reason after his first reason at all.

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ قَدِيرٌ﴾, "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful." Its parallel is in Surat al-Hajj [Surat al-Hajj: 5].

﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ فِي الرِّزْقِ﴾, "And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. So those who have been favoured in provision will not give their provision ﴿عَلَى مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ﴾, "to what their right hands possess", of the slaves, so that they and their slaves would be equal in that." Allah, may His praise be exalted, says: they do not accept that they and their slaves be equal in what We have provided them, yet they have made My servants partners in My dominion and My authority. This parable is used to establish the proof against the polytheists. This is a parable which Allah, mighty and majestic, has coined: none of you shares his slave's wife, his relatives or his wealth with him. Will you then equate with Allah His creation and His servants? If you do not accept this for yourselves, then Allah is more worthy to be exalted above it, and do not equate any of His servants or creatures with Him [see Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/188].

'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: this verse was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran when they said: "Jesus is the son of God." It says: the master does not give back from what his right hand possesses from what He has provided, until the master and the owned are equal in the means of livelihood. How then do you accept for Me what you do not accept for yourselves? Its parallel is in Surat al-Rum: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [Surat al-Rum: 28] [a parable you witness].

He said: ﴿أَفَبِنِعْمَةِ اللَّهِ يَجْحَدُونَ﴾, "Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?" by associating others with Him.

'Asim read with the ta' (tajhadun, in the second person), because of His saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ﴾ and ﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ﴾.

The rest read with the ya' (yajhadun, in the third person), because of His saying: ﴿فَهُمْ فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ﴾ [Surat al-Nahl: 71], and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because the reported party is closer to it.

﴿وَاللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا﴾, "And Allah made for you spouses from yourselves", meaning that He created from Adam his wife Hawwa'. ﴿وَجَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَزْوَاجِكُمْ بَنِينَ وَحَفَدَةً﴾, "and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren."

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Ad'ha said: the hafadah are the in-laws, the husband's sons-in-law (who are married to his daughters).

Shu'bah related from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, who said: I heard Zirr ibn Hubaysh, a foreigner who had lived through the Jahiliyyah, say: "I used to hold the Mushaf for 'Abd Allah, and he came to this verse, and he asked: 'Do you know what al-hafadah are?' I said: 'They are a man's entourage.' 'Abd Allah said: 'No, but they are the in-laws.'" This is also the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: they are the servants.

Mujahid and Abu Malik al-Ansari said: they are the helpers. This is the narration of Abu Hamzah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Whoever helps you is your hafad."

A poet said:

"The young servants surround them, and they hand over
With their hands the reins of the camels."

'Ata' said: they are the man's children who help him, serve him, support him and attend to him.

Qatadah said: they are the servants, the ones who serve you among your children.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the banun (sons) are the young ones, and the hafadah are the older children who help him in his work.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the children's children.

Ibn Zayd said: they are the sons of the wife from her first husband. This is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the sons of a man's first wife.

Al-'Utbi said: the origin of hafd is racing toward danger and hastening in walking.

So it is said of everyone who hastens in service and work: hafadah, its singular being hafid. From this comes the supplication of the witr prayer: "To You we strive and hasten," meaning we hasten to work in Your obedience.

Ibn Jarir recited [for al-Ra'i]:

"I burdened with its unknown things Yamani she-camels
When the drivers hasten on their backs."

﴿وَرَزَقَكُمْ مِنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ﴾, "and provided you with good things. ﴿أَفَبِالْبَاطِلِ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾", "Then do they believe in falsehood?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: in idols.

﴿مِنْ بَيْنِ فَرْثٍ﴾, "from between dung", which is what is in the paunch; when it leaves it, it is no longer called فرث (farth). ﴿وَدَمٍ﴾, "and blood", ﴿لَبَنًا خَالِصًا﴾, "pure milk", purified from the dung and the blood and not mixed with them, ﴿سَائِغًا لِلشَّارِبِينَ﴾, "palatable to the drinkers", ready, pleasant, sliding down the throat without choking its drinker. It was said: no one has ever choked on milk.

Ibn 'Abbas said: when the animal eats the fodder and it settles in its paunch at that time, its lowest part is dung, its middle is milk, and its uppermost part is the blood of the liver. [So what was] of these three kinds is divided: the blood flows in the veins, the milk flows into the udder, and the dung remains as it is.

﴿وَمِنْ ثَمَرَاتِ النَّخِيلِ وَالْأَعْنَابِ﴾, meaning: this too is a lesson, in what We give you to drink and provide you with, from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes, ﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنْهُ﴾, "you take from it". The pronoun in His saying ﴿مِنْهُ﴾ refers back to those mentioned.

﴿سَكَرًا وَرِزْقًا حَسَنًا﴾, "intoxicant and good provision".

Some people said: al-sakar is wine, and al-rizq al-hasan is vinegar, grapes, dates and raisins. They said: this is the view on the prohibition of wine, and this view was held by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Amr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ayyub, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla and al-Kalbi. It is the narration of 'Amr ibn Sufyan al-Basri from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-sakar is what is forbidden of its fruit, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is lawful of its fruit.

As for al-sakar, it is the intoxicants of these foreigners, and as for al-rizq al-hasan, it is what you soak, what you make vinegar from, and what you eat.

He said: this verse was revealed when wine had not yet been forbidden, and its prohibition was revealed after that in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Al-Sha'bi said: al-sakar is what is drunk, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is eaten.

Al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas that the Abyssinians call vinegar al-sakar.

Others said: al-sakar is intoxicating nabidh, which is the steeped infusion of dates and raisins when it has fermented, and the boiled-down juice. This is the view of al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi, according to the narration of Mujalid, and Abu Rawq, and the view of al-Nakha'i, and the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: it is date nabidh.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Wine is what is made from grapes, sakar is from dates, bit' is from honey, mizr is from maize, [and al-bira] [as in the manuscript, though it is not found in the source] from wheat, and I forbid you from every intoxicant." [6] [Musnad Abi Ya'la, 13/216, with variation.]

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-sakar means taste; it is said: "This is sakar for you," meaning a taste for you.

He recited:

"I made the faults of the noble ones a taste."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾, "Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason."

﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ﴾, "And your Lord inspired the bee." That is, He cast [into its ears] or threw into its souls, and it understood it. The nahl (bee) is the wasps of honey, and its singular is nahlah.

﴿أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ﴾, "that take for yourselves houses in the mountains, in the trees, and in what they build". Ibn Zayd said: it means the vineyard.

﴿ثُمَّ كُلِي مِنْ كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ﴾, "Then eat from all the fruits". The meaning of "all" is not generality; it is like His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾, and His saying: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾.

﴿فَاسْلُكِي سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًا﴾, "So follow the ways of your Lord, submissively." That is, enter the paths of your Lord.

Some said: al-dhulul means the paths, and it is said they are made easy for the bees. Mujahid said: "No place is difficult for them that they have traveled."

Others said: al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees [in Tafsir al-Tabari (14/184): it is an attribute of the paths, attributed to Mujahid, then he mentioned the view that al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees, and he preferred the first].

Qatadah and others said: it means obedient and submissive.

﴿يَخْرُجُ مِنْ بُطُونِهَا شَرَابٌ مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ﴾, "From their bellies comes a drink of varying colours", white, red and yellow, ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾, "in it is healing for mankind."

It is related that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My brother has a pain in his stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." He went and came back and said: "I gave him to drink, and it did not help him at all." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Go and give him honey to drink, for Allah has spoken the truth and his brother's stomach has lied." [7] [Sahih Muslim, 7/26, and Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3/276.] So he gave him to drink, and it was as if he had been released from a fetter. [It was related by] 'Atiyyah from Abu al-Mutawakkil from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Mujahid said: ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ means in the Qur'an. The first view is more correct and better suited to the apparent sense of the Book.

Waki' related from Sufyan from Abu Ishaq from Abu al-Ahwas from 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), who said: honey is a healing from every disease, and the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts.

Al-A'mash from Khaytham from al-Aswad said: 'Abd Allah said: "Keep to the two healings: honey and the Qur'an."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾, that is, in what we have mentioned, ﴿لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾, "a sign for a people who reflect", so that they may take lesson.

﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ ثُمَّ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ﴾, "And Allah created you, then He takes you back", as children, youths and elders. ﴿وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرَدُّ إِلَى أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ﴾, "And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age", that is, its worst. It is said from this: "the man became base and despicable (dhall al-rajul wa-fasal, yarthul rudhalah wa-rudhulah, wa-radhalthuhu ana)" [Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/186].

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means to the lowest of life.

Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: it means senility.

Qatadah said: the most abject age is seventy years.

Al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: the most abject age is seventy-five years.

﴿لِكَيْ لَا يَعْلَمَ بَعْدَ عِلْمٍ شَيْئًا﴾, "so that he knows nothing after knowing", that is, he does not reason after his first reason at all.

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ قَدِيرٌ﴾, "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful." Its parallel is in Surat al-Hajj [Surat al-Hajj: 5].

﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ فِي الرِّزْقِ﴾, "And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. So those who have been favoured in provision will not give their provision ﴿عَلَى مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ﴾, "to what their right hands possess", of the slaves, so that they and their slaves would be equal in that." Allah, may His praise be exalted, says: they do not accept that they and their slaves be equal in what We have provided them, yet they have made My servants partners in My dominion and My authority. This parable is used to establish the proof against the polytheists. This is a parable which Allah, mighty and majestic, has coined: none of you shares his slave's wife, his relatives or his wealth with him. Will you then equate with Allah His creation and His servants? If you do not accept this for yourselves, then Allah is more worthy to be exalted above it, and do not equate any of His servants or creatures with Him [see Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/188].

'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: this verse was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran when they said: "Jesus is the son of God." It says: the master does not give back from what his right hand possesses from what He has provided, until the master and the owned are equal in the means of livelihood. How then do you accept for Me what you do not accept for yourselves? Its parallel is in Surat al-Rum: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [Surat al-Rum: 28] [a parable you witness].

He said: ﴿أَفَبِنِعْمَةِ اللَّهِ يَجْحَدُونَ﴾, "Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?" by associating others with Him.

'Asim read with the ta' (tajhadun, in the second person), because of His saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ﴾ and ﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ﴾.

The rest read with the ya' (yajhadun, in the third person), because of His saying: ﴿فَهُمْ فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ﴾ [Surat al-Nahl: 71], and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because the reported party is closer to it.

﴿وَاللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا﴾, "And Allah made for you spouses from yourselves", meaning that He created from Adam his wife Hawwa'. ﴿وَجَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَزْوَاجِكُمْ بَنِينَ وَحَفَدَةً﴾, "and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren."

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Ad'ha said: the hafadah are the in-laws, the husband's sons-in-law (who are married to his daughters).

Shu'bah related from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, who said: I heard Zirr ibn Hubaysh, a foreigner who had lived through the Jahiliyyah, say: "I used to hold the Mushaf for 'Abd Allah, and he came to this verse, and he asked: 'Do you know what al-hafadah are?' I said: 'They are a man's entourage.' 'Abd Allah said: 'No, but they are the in-laws.'" This is also the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: they are the servants.

Mujahid and Abu Malik al-Ansari said: they are the helpers. This is the narration of Abu Hamzah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Whoever helps you is your hafad."

A poet said:

"The young servants surround them, and they hand over
With their hands the reins of the camels."

'Ata' said: they are the man's children who help him, serve him, support him and attend to him.

Qatadah said: they are the servants, the ones who serve you among your children.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the banun (sons) are the young ones, and the hafadah are the older children who help him in his work.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the children's children.

Ibn Zayd said: they are the sons of the wife from her first husband. This is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the sons of a man's first wife.

Al-'Utbi said: the origin of hafd is racing toward danger and hastening in walking.

So it is said of everyone who hastens in service and work: hafadah, its singular being hafid. From this comes the supplication of the witr prayer: "To You we strive and hasten," meaning we hasten to work in Your obedience.

Ibn Jarir recited [for al-Ra'i]:

"I burdened with its unknown things Yamani she-camels
When the drivers hasten on their backs."

﴿وَرَزَقَكُمْ مِنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ﴾, "and provided you with good things. ﴿أَفَبِالْبَاطِلِ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾", "Then do they believe in falsehood?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: in idols.

﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, that is, the false monotheism; the devil commanded them to slaughter the baheerah, the saa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham. ﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ﴾, by what Allah made lawful for them, ﴿هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, they deny, they reject its being made lawful.

﴿وَيَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَمْلِكُ لَهُمْ رِزْقًا مِنَ السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾, that is, the rain, ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾, that is, the plants.

﴿شَيْئًا﴾. Al-Akhfash said: it is a substitute for rizq, and it has the meaning: they do not own any provision, a little or a lot. Al-Farra' said: shay'an (anything) is in the accusative because the word rizq is applied to it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [Surat al-Mursalat: 25-26], meaning it gathers the living and the dead. Similarly His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan near of kin﴾ [Surat al-Balad: 14-15].

﴿وَلَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ﴾, "and they are not able", that is, they have no power over anything. ﴿فَلَا تَضْرِبُوا لِلَّهِ الْأَمْثَالَ﴾, "So do not coin parables for Allah", that is, similitudes and likenesses, lest they liken Him to His creation and make a partner for Him, for He is One with no like. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ﴾, "Indeed Allah knows" the error of what they coin of parables for Him, ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, "and you do not know" the correctness of that from its error.

﴿And Allah sends down from the sky water﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and He revives the earth after its death﴾, after its barrenness and its being worn out. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen﴾, with the hearing of the hearts and not the hearing of the ears.

﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾, an admonition. ﴿We give you to drink﴾.

The people of Medina, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and 'Asim read ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ﴾ with a fatha on the nun (nasqikum).

The rest read it with a damma on the nun (nusqikum), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, saying: "Because it is a drink that is continuous."

It is related from al-Kisa'i that the Arabs say أسقيته نهرا (asqaytuhu nahran, "I gave him a river to water him") and أسقيته لبنا (asqaytuhu laban, "I gave him milk") when they mean to provide a continuous supply, but when they mean that they gave him a single drink, they say سقيناه (saqaynahu), without the alif.

Others said: "They are two dialects, and what indicates this is the saying of Labid in describing the watering:

"He gave drink to my people, the Banu Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilal."

He combined the two dialects.

﴿مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "from what is in their bellies", and he did not say بطونها (butuniha), although الأنعام (al-an'am, the livestock) is a plural. Al-Mubarrad said: the pronoun refers to النعم (al-ni'am, "the cattle"), and النعم and الأنعام are one and the same, and the word النعم is used. He cited in evidence a rajaz verse of one of the Bedouin:

"When you see the stars of Leo
Rise over its forehead and the khara and the kanad,
And Suhayl sets at al-Fadih, and it becomes spoiled,
And the milk of the she-camels becomes good and cool."

He did not say فبردت (fabaradat), because he referred it back to اللبن (al-laban, "the milk") or الخراة (al-kharah). [Thus in the original.]

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: نعم (ni'am, "cattle") is masculine and feminine. Whoever makes it feminine does so for the sense of plurality, and whoever makes it masculine does so for the form of the word, and because it has no singular from its own form.

A poet said about it:

"Every year there are cattle that you keep,
A people impregnate them and you deliver them,
Indeed they have palm trees, so they do not protect them."

Al-Kisa'i said: the pronoun refers back to what is intended, in the bellies of what has been mentioned.

Some of them said: he meant the bellies of this thing, like Allah's saying: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord"﴾, and His saying: ﴿"And indeed I am sending a gift to them"﴾ up to ﴿So when he came to Solomon﴾, and He did not say "she came."

Al-Salt al-'Abdi said:

"Indeed, generosity and manliness have enclosed
A grave in Marw, on the clear road."

Another said:

"And 'Afra' is the nearest of people to me in affection,
And 'Afra' is far from me, the one who turns away and holds back."

Another said:

"When people are people and the lands are in prosperity,
And the mother of 'Ammar is a friend who helps."

All of that is according to the meaning of this person and this thing.

It is related that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My brother has a pain in his stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." He went and came back and said: "I gave him to drink, and it did not help him at all." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Go and give him honey to drink, for Allah has spoken the truth and his brother's stomach has lied." [7] [Sahih Muslim, 7/26, and Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3/276.] So he gave him to drink, and it was as if he had been released from a fetter. [It was related by] 'Atiyyah from Abu al-Mutawakkil from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Mujahid said: ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ means in the Qur'an. The first view is more correct and better suited to the apparent sense of the Book.

Waki' related from Sufyan from Abu Ishaq from Abu al-Ahwas from 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), who said: honey is a healing from every disease, and the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts.

Al-A'mash from Khaytham from al-Aswad said: 'Abd Allah said: "Keep to the two healings: honey and the Qur'an."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾, that is, in what we have mentioned, ﴿لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾, "a sign for a people who reflect", so that they may take lesson.

﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ ثُمَّ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ﴾, "And Allah created you, then He takes you back", as children, youths and elders. ﴿وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرَدُّ إِلَى أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ﴾, "And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age", that is, its worst. It is said from this: "the man became base and despicable (dhall al-rajul wa-fasal, yarthul rudhalah wa-rudhulah, wa-radhalthuhu ana)" [Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/186].

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means to the lowest of life.

Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: it means senility.

Qatadah said: the most abject age is seventy years.

Al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: the most abject age is seventy-five years.

﴿لِكَيْ لَا يَعْلَمَ بَعْدَ عِلْمٍ شَيْئًا﴾, "so that he knows nothing after knowing", that is, he does not reason after his first reason at all.

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ قَدِيرٌ﴾, "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful." Its parallel is in Surat al-Hajj [Surat al-Hajj: 5].

﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ فِي الرِّزْقِ﴾, "And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. So those who have been favoured in provision will not give their provision ﴿عَلَى مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ﴾, "to what their right hands possess", of the slaves, so that they and their slaves would be equal in that." Allah, may His praise be exalted, says: they do not accept that they and their slaves be equal in what We have provided them, yet they have made My servants partners in My dominion and My authority. This parable is used to establish the proof against the polytheists. This is a parable which Allah, mighty and majestic, has coined: none of you shares his slave's wife, his relatives or his wealth with him. Will you then equate with Allah His creation and His servants? If you do not accept this for yourselves, then Allah is more worthy to be exalted above it, and do not equate any of His servants or creatures with Him [see Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/188].

'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: this verse was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran when they said: "Jesus is the son of God." It says: the master does not give back from what his right hand possesses from what He has provided, until the master and the owned are equal in the means of livelihood. How then do you accept for Me what you do not accept for yourselves? Its parallel is in Surat al-Rum: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [Surat al-Rum: 28] [a parable you witness].

He said: ﴿أَفَبِنِعْمَةِ اللَّهِ يَجْحَدُونَ﴾, "Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?" by associating others with Him.

'Asim read with the ta' (tajhadun, in the second person), because of His saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ﴾ and ﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ﴾.

The rest read with the ya' (yajhadun, in the third person), because of His saying: ﴿فَهُمْ فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ﴾ [Surat al-Nahl: 71], and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because the reported party is closer to it.

﴿وَاللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا﴾, "And Allah made for you spouses from yourselves", meaning that He created from Adam his wife Hawwa'. ﴿وَجَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَزْوَاجِكُمْ بَنِينَ وَحَفَدَةً﴾, "and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren."

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Ad'ha said: the hafadah are the in-laws, the husband's sons-in-law (who are married to his daughters).

Shu'bah related from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, who said: I heard Zirr ibn Hubaysh, a foreigner who had lived through the Jahiliyyah, say: "I used to hold the Mushaf for 'Abd Allah, and he came to this verse, and he asked: 'Do you know what al-hafadah are?' I said: 'They are a man's entourage.' 'Abd Allah said: 'No, but they are the in-laws.'" This is also the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: they are the servants.

Mujahid and Abu Malik al-Ansari said: they are the helpers. This is the narration of Abu Hamzah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Whoever helps you is your hafad."

A poet said:

"The young servants surround them, and they hand over
With their hands the reins of the camels."

'Ata' said: they are the man's children who help him, serve him, support him and attend to him.

Qatadah said: they are the servants, the ones who serve you among your children.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the banun (sons) are the young ones, and the hafadah are the older children who help him in his work.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the children's children.

Ibn Zayd said: they are the sons of the wife from her first husband. This is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the sons of a man's first wife.

Al-'Utbi said: the origin of hafd is racing toward danger and hastening in walking.

So it is said of everyone who hastens in service and work: hafadah, its singular being hafid. From this comes the supplication of the witr prayer: "To You we strive and hasten," meaning we hasten to work in Your obedience.

Ibn Jarir recited [for al-Ra'i]:

"I burdened with its unknown things Yamani she-camels
When the drivers hasten on their backs."

﴿وَرَزَقَكُمْ مِنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ﴾, "and provided you with good things. ﴿أَفَبِالْبَاطِلِ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾", "Then do they believe in falsehood?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: in idols.

﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, that is, the false monotheism; the devil commanded them to slaughter the baheerah, the saa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham. ﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ﴾, by what Allah made lawful for them, ﴿هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, they deny, they reject its being made lawful.

﴿وَيَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَمْلِكُ لَهُمْ رِزْقًا مِنَ السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾, that is, the rain, ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾, that is, the plants.

﴿شَيْئًا﴾. Al-Akhfash said: it is a substitute for rizq, and it has the meaning: they do not own any provision, a little or a lot. Al-Farra' said: shay'an (anything) is in the accusative because the word rizq is applied to it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [Surat al-Mursalat: 25-26], meaning it gathers the living and the dead. Similarly His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan near of kin﴾ [Surat al-Balad: 14-15].

﴿وَلَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ﴾, "and they are not able", that is, they have no power over anything. ﴿فَلَا تَضْرِبُوا لِلَّهِ الْأَمْثَالَ﴾, "So do not coin parables for Allah", that is, similitudes and likenesses, lest they liken Him to His creation and make a partner for Him, for He is One with no like. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ﴾, "Indeed Allah knows" the error of what they coin of parables for Him, ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, "and you do not know" the correctness of that from its error.

﴿And Allah sends down from the sky water﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and He revives the earth after its death﴾, after its barrenness and its being worn out. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen﴾, with the hearing of the hearts and not the hearing of the ears.

﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾, an admonition. ﴿We give you to drink﴾.

The people of Medina, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and 'Asim read ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ﴾ with a fatha on the nun (nasqikum).

The rest read it with a damma on the nun (nusqikum), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, saying: "Because it is a drink that is continuous."

It is related from al-Kisa'i that the Arabs say أسقيته نهرا (asqaytuhu nahran, "I gave him a river to water him") and أسقيته لبنا (asqaytuhu laban, "I gave him milk") when they mean to provide a continuous supply, but when they mean that they gave him a single drink, they say سقيناه (saqaynahu), without the alif.

Others said: "They are two dialects, and what indicates this is the saying of Labid in describing the watering:

"He gave drink to my people, the Banu Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilal."

He combined the two dialects.

﴿مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "from what is in their bellies", and he did not say بطونها (butuniha), although الأنعام (al-an'am, the livestock) is a plural. Al-Mubarrad said: the pronoun refers to النعم (al-ni'am, "the cattle"), and النعم and الأنعام are one and the same, and the word النعم is used. He cited in evidence a rajaz verse of one of the Bedouin:

"When you see the stars of Leo
Rise over its forehead and the khara and the kanad,
And Suhayl sets at al-Fadih, and it becomes spoiled,
And the milk of the she-camels becomes good and cool."

He did not say فبردت (fabaradat), because he referred it back to اللبن (al-laban, "the milk") or الخراة (al-kharah). [Thus in the original.]

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: نعم (ni'am, "cattle") is masculine and feminine. Whoever makes it feminine does so for the sense of plurality, and whoever makes it masculine does so for the form of the word, and because it has no singular from its own form.

A poet said about it:

"Every year there are cattle that you keep,
A people impregnate them and you deliver them,
Indeed they have palm trees, so they do not protect them."

Al-Kisa'i said: the pronoun refers back to what is intended, in the bellies of what has been mentioned.

Some of them said: he meant the bellies of this thing, like Allah's saying: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord"﴾, and His saying: ﴿"And indeed I am sending a gift to them"﴾ up to ﴿So when he came to Solomon﴾, and He did not say "she came."

Al-Salt al-'Abdi said:

"Indeed, generosity and manliness have enclosed
A grave in Marw, on the clear road."

Another said:

"And 'Afra' is the nearest of people to me in affection,
And 'Afra' is far from me, the one who turns away and holds back."

Another said:

"When people are people and the lands are in prosperity,
And the mother of 'Ammar is a friend who helps."

All of that is according to the meaning of this person and this thing.

Al-Mu'arrij said: the pronoun refers back to the part and the portion, as if He said: ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "We give you to drink from what is in their bellies," which is the milk, since not all of them have milk, but only those that have milk are watered, so the milk is implied in it.

﴿مِنْ بَيْنِ فَرْثٍ﴾, "from between dung", which is what is in the paunch; when it leaves it, it is no longer called فرث (farth). ﴿وَدَمٍ﴾, "and blood", ﴿لَبَنًا خَالِصًا﴾, "pure milk", purified from the dung and the blood and not mixed with them, ﴿سَائِغًا لِلشَّارِبِينَ﴾, "palatable to the drinkers", ready, pleasant, sliding down the throat without choking its drinker. It was said: no one has ever choked on milk.

Ibn 'Abbas said: when the animal eats the fodder and it settles in its paunch at that time, its lowest part is dung, its middle is milk, and its uppermost part is the blood of the liver. [So what was] of these three kinds is divided: the blood flows in the veins, the milk flows into the udder, and the dung remains as it is.

﴿وَمِنْ ثَمَرَاتِ النَّخِيلِ وَالْأَعْنَابِ﴾, meaning: this too is a lesson, in what We give you to drink and provide you with, from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes, ﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنْهُ﴾, "you take from it". The pronoun in His saying ﴿مِنْهُ﴾ refers back to those mentioned.

﴿سَكَرًا وَرِزْقًا حَسَنًا﴾, "intoxicant and good provision".

Some people said: al-sakar is wine, and al-rizq al-hasan is vinegar, grapes, dates and raisins. They said: this is the view on the prohibition of wine, and this view was held by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Amr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ayyub, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla and al-Kalbi. It is the narration of 'Amr ibn Sufyan al-Basri from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-sakar is what is forbidden of its fruit, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is lawful of its fruit.

As for al-sakar, it is the intoxicants of these foreigners, and as for al-rizq al-hasan, it is what you soak, what you make vinegar from, and what you eat.

He said: this verse was revealed when wine had not yet been forbidden, and its prohibition was revealed after that in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Al-Sha'bi said: al-sakar is what is drunk, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is eaten.

Al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas that the Abyssinians call vinegar al-sakar.

Others said: al-sakar is intoxicating nabidh, which is the steeped infusion of dates and raisins when it has fermented, and the boiled-down juice. This is the view of al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi, according to the narration of Mujalid, and Abu Rawq, and the view of al-Nakha'i, and the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: it is date nabidh.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Wine is what is made from grapes, sakar is from dates, bit' is from honey, mizr is from maize, [and al-bira] [as in the manuscript, though it is not found in the source] from wheat, and I forbid you from every intoxicant." [6] [Musnad Abi Ya'la, 13/216, with variation.]

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-sakar means taste; it is said: "This is sakar for you," meaning a taste for you.

He recited:

"I made the faults of the noble ones a taste."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾, "Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason."

﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ﴾, "And your Lord inspired the bee." That is, He cast [into its ears] or threw into its souls, and it understood it. The nahl (bee) is the wasps of honey, and its singular is nahlah.

﴿أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ﴾, "that take for yourselves houses in the mountains, in the trees, and in what they build". Ibn Zayd said: it means the vineyard.

﴿ثُمَّ كُلِي مِنْ كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ﴾, "Then eat from all the fruits". The meaning of "all" is not generality; it is like His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾, and His saying: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾.

﴿فَاسْلُكِي سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًا﴾, "So follow the ways of your Lord, submissively." That is, enter the paths of your Lord.

Some said: al-dhulul means the paths, and it is said they are made easy for the bees. Mujahid said: "No place is difficult for them that they have traveled."

Others said: al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees [in Tafsir al-Tabari (14/184): it is an attribute of the paths, attributed to Mujahid, then he mentioned the view that al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees, and he preferred the first].

Qatadah and others said: it means obedient and submissive.

﴿يَخْرُجُ مِنْ بُطُونِهَا شَرَابٌ مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ﴾, "From their bellies comes a drink of varying colours", white, red and yellow, ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾, "in it is healing for mankind."

It is related that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My brother has a pain in his stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." He went and came back and said: "I gave him to drink, and it did not help him at all." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Go and give him honey to drink, for Allah has spoken the truth and his brother's stomach has lied." [7] [Sahih Muslim, 7/26, and Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3/276.] So he gave him to drink, and it was as if he had been released from a fetter. [It was related by] 'Atiyyah from Abu al-Mutawakkil from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.
