Shu'bah related from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, who said: I heard Zirr ibn Hubaysh, a foreigner who had lived through the Jahiliyyah, say: "I used to hold the Mushaf for 'Abd Allah, and he came to this verse, and he asked: 'Do you know what al-hafadah are?' I said: 'They are a man's entourage.' 'Abd Allah said: 'No, but they are the in-laws.'" This is also the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: they are the servants.

Mujahid and Abu Malik al-Ansari said: they are the helpers. This is the narration of Abu Hamzah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Whoever helps you is your hafad."

A poet said:

"The young servants surround them, and they hand over
With their hands the reins of the camels."

'Ata' said: they are the man's children who help him, serve him, support him and attend to him.

Qatadah said: they are the servants, the ones who serve you among your children.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the banun (sons) are the young ones, and the hafadah are the older children who help him in his work.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the children's children.

Ibn Zayd said: they are the sons of the wife from her first husband. This is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the sons of a man's first wife.

Al-'Utbi said: the origin of hafd is racing toward danger and hastening in walking.

So it is said of everyone who hastens in service and work: hafadah, its singular being hafid. From this comes the supplication of the witr prayer: "To You we strive and hasten," meaning we hasten to work in Your obedience.

Ibn Jarir recited [for al-Ra'i]:

"I burdened with its unknown things Yamani she-camels
When the drivers hasten on their backs."

﴿وَرَزَقَكُمْ مِنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ﴾, "and provided you with good things. ﴿أَفَبِالْبَاطِلِ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾", "Then do they believe in falsehood?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: in idols.

﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, that is, the false monotheism; the devil commanded them to slaughter the baheerah, the saa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham. ﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ﴾, by what Allah made lawful for them, ﴿هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, they deny, they reject its being made lawful.

﴿وَيَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَمْلِكُ لَهُمْ رِزْقًا مِنَ السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾, that is, the rain, ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾, that is, the plants.

﴿شَيْئًا﴾. Al-Akhfash said: it is a substitute for rizq, and it has the meaning: they do not own any provision, a little or a lot. Al-Farra' said: shay'an (anything) is in the accusative because the word rizq is applied to it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [Surat al-Mursalat: 25-26], meaning it gathers the living and the dead. Similarly His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan near of kin﴾ [Surat al-Balad: 14-15].

﴿وَلَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ﴾, "and they are not able", that is, they have no power over anything. ﴿فَلَا تَضْرِبُوا لِلَّهِ الْأَمْثَالَ﴾, "So do not coin parables for Allah", that is, similitudes and likenesses, lest they liken Him to His creation and make a partner for Him, for He is One with no like. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ﴾, "Indeed Allah knows" the error of what they coin of parables for Him, ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, "and you do not know" the correctness of that from its error.

﴿And Allah sends down from the sky water﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and He revives the earth after its death﴾, after its barrenness and its being worn out. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen﴾, with the hearing of the hearts and not the hearing of the ears.

﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾, an admonition. ﴿We give you to drink﴾.

The people of Medina, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and 'Asim read ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ﴾ with a fatha on the nun (nasqikum).

The rest read it with a damma on the nun (nusqikum), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, saying: "Because it is a drink that is continuous."

It is related from al-Kisa'i that the Arabs say أسقيته نهرا (asqaytuhu nahran, "I gave him a river to water him") and أسقيته لبنا (asqaytuhu laban, "I gave him milk") when they mean to provide a continuous supply, but when they mean that they gave him a single drink, they say سقيناه (saqaynahu), without the alif.

Others said: "They are two dialects, and what indicates this is the saying of Labid in describing the watering:

"He gave drink to my people, the Banu Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilal."

He combined the two dialects.

﴿مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "from what is in their bellies", and he did not say بطونها (butuniha), although الأنعام (al-an'am, the livestock) is a plural. Al-Mubarrad said: the pronoun refers to النعم (al-ni'am, "the cattle"), and النعم and الأنعام are one and the same, and the word النعم is used. He cited in evidence a rajaz verse of one of the Bedouin:

"When you see the stars of Leo
Rise over its forehead and the khara and the kanad,
And Suhayl sets at al-Fadih, and it becomes spoiled,
And the milk of the she-camels becomes good and cool."

He did not say فبردت (fabaradat), because he referred it back to اللبن (al-laban, "the milk") or الخراة (al-kharah). [Thus in the original.]

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: نعم (ni'am, "cattle") is masculine and feminine. Whoever makes it feminine does so for the sense of plurality, and whoever makes it masculine does so for the form of the word, and because it has no singular from its own form.

A poet said about it:

"Every year there are cattle that you keep,
A people impregnate them and you deliver them,
Indeed they have palm trees, so they do not protect them."

Al-Kisa'i said: the pronoun refers back to what is intended, in the bellies of what has been mentioned.

Some of them said: he meant the bellies of this thing, like Allah's saying: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord"﴾, and His saying: ﴿"And indeed I am sending a gift to them"﴾ up to ﴿So when he came to Solomon﴾, and He did not say "she came."

Al-Salt al-'Abdi said:

"Indeed, generosity and manliness have enclosed
A grave in Marw, on the clear road."

Another said:

"And 'Afra' is the nearest of people to me in affection,
And 'Afra' is far from me, the one who turns away and holds back."

Another said:

"When people are people and the lands are in prosperity,
And the mother of 'Ammar is a friend who helps."

All of that is according to the meaning of this person and this thing.

Al-Mu'arrij said: the pronoun refers back to the part and the portion, as if He said: ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "We give you to drink from what is in their bellies," which is the milk, since not all of them have milk, but only those that have milk are watered, so the milk is implied in it.

﴿مِنْ بَيْنِ فَرْثٍ﴾, "from between dung", which is what is in the paunch; when it leaves it, it is no longer called فرث (farth). ﴿وَدَمٍ﴾, "and blood", ﴿لَبَنًا خَالِصًا﴾, "pure milk", purified from the dung and the blood and not mixed with them, ﴿سَائِغًا لِلشَّارِبِينَ﴾, "palatable to the drinkers", ready, pleasant, sliding down the throat without choking its drinker. It was said: no one has ever choked on milk.

Ibn 'Abbas said: when the animal eats the fodder and it settles in its paunch at that time, its lowest part is dung, its middle is milk, and its uppermost part is the blood of the liver. [So what was] of these three kinds is divided: the blood flows in the veins, the milk flows into the udder, and the dung remains as it is.

﴿وَمِنْ ثَمَرَاتِ النَّخِيلِ وَالْأَعْنَابِ﴾, meaning: this too is a lesson, in what We give you to drink and provide you with, from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes, ﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنْهُ﴾, "you take from it". The pronoun in His saying ﴿مِنْهُ﴾ refers back to those mentioned.

﴿سَكَرًا وَرِزْقًا حَسَنًا﴾, "intoxicant and good provision".

Some people said: al-sakar is wine, and al-rizq al-hasan is vinegar, grapes, dates and raisins. They said: this is the view on the prohibition of wine, and this view was held by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Amr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ayyub, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla and al-Kalbi. It is the narration of 'Amr ibn Sufyan al-Basri from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-sakar is what is forbidden of its fruit, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is lawful of its fruit.

As for al-sakar, it is the intoxicants of these foreigners, and as for al-rizq al-hasan, it is what you soak, what you make vinegar from, and what you eat.

He said: this verse was revealed when wine had not yet been forbidden, and its prohibition was revealed after that in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Al-Sha'bi said: al-sakar is what is drunk, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is eaten.

Al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas that the Abyssinians call vinegar al-sakar.

Others said: al-sakar is intoxicating nabidh, which is the steeped infusion of dates and raisins when it has fermented, and the boiled-down juice. This is the view of al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi, according to the narration of Mujalid, and Abu Rawq, and the view of al-Nakha'i, and the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: it is date nabidh.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Wine is what is made from grapes, sakar is from dates, bit' is from honey, mizr is from maize, [and al-bira] [as in the manuscript, though it is not found in the source] from wheat, and I forbid you from every intoxicant." [6] [Musnad Abi Ya'la, 13/216, with variation.]

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-sakar means taste; it is said: "This is sakar for you," meaning a taste for you.

He recited:

"I made the faults of the noble ones a taste."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾, "Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason."

﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ﴾, "And your Lord inspired the bee." That is, He cast [into its ears] or threw into its souls, and it understood it. The nahl (bee) is the wasps of honey, and its singular is nahlah.

﴿أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ﴾, "that take for yourselves houses in the mountains, in the trees, and in what they build". Ibn Zayd said: it means the vineyard.

﴿ثُمَّ كُلِي مِنْ كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ﴾, "Then eat from all the fruits". The meaning of "all" is not generality; it is like His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾, and His saying: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾.

﴿فَاسْلُكِي سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًا﴾, "So follow the ways of your Lord, submissively." That is, enter the paths of your Lord.

Some said: al-dhulul means the paths, and it is said they are made easy for the bees. Mujahid said: "No place is difficult for them that they have traveled."

Others said: al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees [in Tafsir al-Tabari (14/184): it is an attribute of the paths, attributed to Mujahid, then he mentioned the view that al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees, and he preferred the first].

Qatadah and others said: it means obedient and submissive.

﴿يَخْرُجُ مِنْ بُطُونِهَا شَرَابٌ مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ﴾, "From their bellies comes a drink of varying colours", white, red and yellow, ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾, "in it is healing for mankind."

It is related that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My brother has a pain in his stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." He went and came back and said: "I gave him to drink, and it did not help him at all." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Go and give him honey to drink, for Allah has spoken the truth and his brother's stomach has lied." [7] [Sahih Muslim, 7/26, and Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3/276.] So he gave him to drink, and it was as if he had been released from a fetter. [It was related by] 'Atiyyah from Abu al-Mutawakkil from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Mujahid said: ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ means in the Qur'an. The first view is more correct and better suited to the apparent sense of the Book.

Waki' related from Sufyan from Abu Ishaq from Abu al-Ahwas from 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), who said: honey is a healing from every disease, and the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts.

Al-A'mash from Khaytham from al-Aswad said: 'Abd Allah said: "Keep to the two healings: honey and the Qur'an."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾, that is, in what we have mentioned, ﴿لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾, "a sign for a people who reflect", so that they may take lesson.

﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ ثُمَّ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ﴾, "And Allah created you, then He takes you back", as children, youths and elders. ﴿وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرَدُّ إِلَى أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ﴾, "And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age", that is, its worst. It is said from this: "the man became base and despicable (dhall al-rajul wa-fasal, yarthul rudhalah wa-rudhulah, wa-radhalthuhu ana)" [Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/186].

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means to the lowest of life.

Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: it means senility.

Qatadah said: the most abject age is seventy years.

Al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: the most abject age is seventy-five years.

﴿لِكَيْ لَا يَعْلَمَ بَعْدَ عِلْمٍ شَيْئًا﴾, "so that he knows nothing after knowing", that is, he does not reason after his first reason at all.

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ قَدِيرٌ﴾, "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful." Its parallel is in Surat al-Hajj [Surat al-Hajj: 5].

﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ فِي الرِّزْقِ﴾, "And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. So those who have been favoured in provision will not give their provision ﴿عَلَى مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ﴾, "to what their right hands possess", of the slaves, so that they and their slaves would be equal in that." Allah, may His praise be exalted, says: they do not accept that they and their slaves be equal in what We have provided them, yet they have made My servants partners in My dominion and My authority. This parable is used to establish the proof against the polytheists. This is a parable which Allah, mighty and majestic, has coined: none of you shares his slave's wife, his relatives or his wealth with him. Will you then equate with Allah His creation and His servants? If you do not accept this for yourselves, then Allah is more worthy to be exalted above it, and do not equate any of His servants or creatures with Him [see Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/188].

'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: this verse was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran when they said: "Jesus is the son of God." It says: the master does not give back from what his right hand possesses from what He has provided, until the master and the owned are equal in the means of livelihood. How then do you accept for Me what you do not accept for yourselves? Its parallel is in Surat al-Rum: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [Surat al-Rum: 28] [a parable you witness].

He said: ﴿أَفَبِنِعْمَةِ اللَّهِ يَجْحَدُونَ﴾, "Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?" by associating others with Him.

'Asim read with the ta' (tajhadun, in the second person), because of His saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ﴾ and ﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ﴾.

The rest read with the ya' (yajhadun, in the third person), because of His saying: ﴿فَهُمْ فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ﴾ [Surat al-Nahl: 71], and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because the reported party is closer to it.

﴿وَاللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا﴾, "And Allah made for you spouses from yourselves", meaning that He created from Adam his wife Hawwa'. ﴿وَجَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَزْوَاجِكُمْ بَنِينَ وَحَفَدَةً﴾, "and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren."

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Ad'ha said: the hafadah are the in-laws, the husband's sons-in-law (who are married to his daughters).

Shu'bah related from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, who said: I heard Zirr ibn Hubaysh, a foreigner who had lived through the Jahiliyyah, say: "I used to hold the Mushaf for 'Abd Allah, and he came to this verse, and he asked: 'Do you know what al-hafadah are?' With their hands the reins of the camels."

Qatadah said: they are the servants, the ones who serve you among your children.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the banun (sons) are the young ones, and the hafadah are the older children who help him in his work.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the children's children.

Ibn Zayd said: they are the sons of the wife from her first husband. This is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the sons of a man's first wife.

He did not say فبردت (fabaradat), because he referred it back to اللبن (al-laban, "the milk") or الخراة (al-kharah). [Thus in the original.]

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: نعم (ni'am, "cattle") is masculine and feminine. Whoever makes it feminine does so for the sense of plurality, and whoever makes it masculine does so for the form of the word, and because it has no singular from its own form.

A poet said about it:

"Every year there are cattle that you keep,
A people impregnate them and you deliver them,
Indeed they have palm trees, so they do not protect them."

Al-Kisa'i said: the pronoun refers back to what is intended, in the bellies of what has been mentioned.

Some of them said: he meant the bellies of this thing, like Allah's saying: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord"﴾, and His saying: ﴿"And indeed I am sending a gift to them"﴾ up to ﴿So when he came to Solomon﴾, and He did not say "she came."

Al-Salt al-'Abdi said:

"Indeed, generosity and manliness have enclosed
A grave in Marw, on the clear road."

Another said:

"And 'Afra' is the nearest of people to me in affection,
And 'Afra' is far from me, the one who turns away and holds back."

Another said:

"When people are people and the lands are in prosperity,
And the mother of 'Ammar is a friend who helps."

All of that is according to the meaning of this person and this thing.

Al-Mu'arrij said: the pronoun refers back to the part and the portion, as if He said: ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "We give you to drink from what is in their bellies," which is the milk, since not all of them have milk, but only those that have milk are watered, so the milk is implied in it.

﴿مِنْ بَيْنِ فَرْثٍ﴾, "from between dung", which is what is in the paunch; when it leaves it, it is no longer called فرث (farth). ﴿وَدَمٍ﴾, "and blood", ﴿لَبَنًا خَالِصًا﴾, "pure milk", purified from the dung and the blood and not mixed with them, ﴿سَائِغًا لِلشَّارِبِينَ﴾, "palatable to the drinkers", ready, pleasant, sliding down the throat without choking its drinker. It was said: no one has ever choked on milk.

Ibn 'Abbas said: when the animal eats the fodder and it settles in its paunch at that time, its lowest part is dung, its middle is milk, and its uppermost part is the blood of the liver. [So what was] of these three kinds is divided: the blood flows in the veins, the milk flows into the udder, and the dung remains as it is.

﴿وَمِنْ ثَمَرَاتِ النَّخِيلِ وَالْأَعْنَابِ﴾, meaning: this too is a lesson, in what We give you to drink and provide you with, from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes, ﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنْهُ﴾, "you take from it". The pronoun in His saying ﴿مِنْهُ﴾ refers back to those mentioned.

﴿سَكَرًا وَرِزْقًا حَسَنًا﴾, "intoxicant and good provision".

Some people said: al-sakar is wine, and al-rizq al-hasan is vinegar, grapes, dates and raisins. They said: this is the view on the prohibition of wine, and this view was held by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Amr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ayyub, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla and al-Kalbi. It is the narration of 'Amr ibn Sufyan al-Basri from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-sakar is what is forbidden of its fruit, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is lawful of its fruit.

As for al-sakar, it is the intoxicants of these foreigners, and as for al-rizq al-hasan, it is what you soak, what you make vinegar from, and what you eat.

He said: this verse was revealed when wine had not yet been forbidden, and its prohibition was revealed after that in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Al-Sha'bi said: al-sakar is what is drunk, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is eaten.

Al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas that the Abyssinians call vinegar al-sakar.

Others said: al-sakar is intoxicating nabidh, which is the steeped infusion of dates and raisins when it has fermented, and the boiled-down juice. This is the view of al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi, according to the narration of Mujalid, and Abu Rawq, and the view of al-Nakha'i, and the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: it is date nabidh.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Wine is what is made from grapes, sakar is from dates, bit' is from honey, mizr is from maize, [and al-bira] [as in the manuscript, though it is not found in the source] from wheat, and I forbid you from every intoxicant." [6] [Musnad Abi Ya'la, 13/216, with variation.]

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-sakar means taste; it is said: "This is sakar for you," meaning a taste for you.

He recited:

"I made the faults of the noble ones a taste."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾, "Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reason."

﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ﴾, "And your Lord inspired the bee." That is, He cast [into its ears] or threw into its souls, and it understood it. The nahl (bee) is the wasps of honey, and its singular is nahlah.

﴿أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ﴾, "that take for yourselves houses in the mountains, in the trees, and in what they build". Ibn Zayd said: it means the vineyard.

﴿ثُمَّ كُلِي مِنْ كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ﴾, "Then eat from all the fruits". The meaning of "all" is not generality; it is like His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾, and His saying: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾.

﴿فَاسْلُكِي سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًا﴾, "So follow the ways of your Lord, submissively." That is, enter the paths of your Lord.

Some said: al-dhulul means the paths, and it is said they are made easy for the bees. Mujahid said: "No place is difficult for them that they have traveled."

Others said: al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees [in Tafsir al-Tabari (14/184): it is an attribute of the paths, attributed to Mujahid, then he mentioned the view that al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees, and he preferred the first].

Qatadah and others said: it means obedient and submissive.

﴿يَخْرُجُ مِنْ بُطُونِهَا شَرَابٌ مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ﴾, "From their bellies comes a drink of varying colours", white, red and yellow, ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾, "in it is healing for mankind."

It is related that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My brother has a pain in his stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." He went and came back and said: "I gave him to drink, and it did not help him at all." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Go and give him honey to drink, for Allah has spoken the truth and his brother's stomach has lied." [7] [Sahih Muslim, 7/26, and Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3/276.] So he gave him to drink, and it was as if he had been released from a fetter. [It was related by] 'Atiyyah from Abu al-Mutawakkil from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Mujahid said: ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ means in the Qur'an. The first view is more correct and better suited to the apparent sense of the Book.

Waki' related from Sufyan from Abu Ishaq from Abu al-Ahwas from 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), who said: honey is a healing from every disease, and the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts.

Al-A'mash from Khaytham from al-Aswad said: 'Abd Allah said: "Keep to the two healings: honey and the Qur'an."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾, that is, in what we have mentioned, ﴿لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾, "a sign for a people who reflect", so that they may take lesson.

﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ ثُمَّ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ﴾, "And Allah created you, then He takes you back", as children, youths and elders. ﴿وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرَدُّ إِلَى أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ﴾, "And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age", that is, its worst. It is said from this: "the man became base and despicable (dhall al-rajul wa-fasal, yarthul rudhalah wa-rudhulah, wa-radhalthuhu ana)" [Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/186].

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means to the lowest of life.

Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: it means senility.

Qatadah said: the most abject age is seventy years.

Al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: the most abject age is seventy-five years.

﴿لِكَيْ لَا يَعْلَمَ بَعْدَ عِلْمٍ شَيْئًا﴾, "so that he knows nothing after knowing", that is, he does not reason after his first reason at all.

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ قَدِيرٌ﴾, "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful." Its parallel is in Surat al-Hajj [Surat al-Hajj: 5].

﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ فِي الرِّزْقِ﴾, "And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. Allah, may His praise be exalted, says: they do not accept that they and their slaves be equal in what We have provided them, yet they have made My servants partners in My dominion and My authority. This parable is used to establish the proof against the polytheists. This is a parable which Allah, mighty and majestic, has coined: none of you shares his slave's wife, his relatives or his wealth with him. Will you then equate with Allah His creation and His servants? If you do not accept this for yourselves, then Allah is more worthy to be exalted above it, and do not equate any of His servants or creatures with Him [see Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/188].

It says: the master does not give back from what his right hand possesses from what He has provided, until the master and the owned are equal in the means of livelihood. How then do you accept for Me what you do not accept for yourselves? Its parallel is in Surat al-Rum: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [Surat al-Rum: 28] [a parable you witness].

He said: ﴿أَفَبِنِعْمَةِ اللَّهِ يَجْحَدُونَ﴾, "Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?" by associating others with Him.

'Asim read with the ta' (tajhadun, in the second person), because of His saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ﴾ and ﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ﴾.

The rest read with the ya' (yajhadun, in the third person), because of His saying: ﴿فَهُمْ فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ﴾ [Surat al-Nahl: 71], and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because the reported party is closer to it.

﴿وَاللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا﴾, "And Allah made for you spouses from yourselves", meaning that He created from Adam his wife Hawwa'. ﴿وَجَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَزْوَاجِكُمْ بَنِينَ وَحَفَدَةً﴾, "and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren."

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Ad'ha said: the hafadah are the in-laws, the husband's sons-in-law (who are married to his daughters).

Shu'bah related from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, who said: I heard Zirr ibn Hubaysh, a foreigner who had lived through the Jahiliyyah, say: "I used to hold the Mushaf for 'Abd Allah, and he came to this verse, and he asked: 'Do you know what al-hafadah are?' I said: 'They are a man's entourage.' 'Abd Allah said: 'No, but they are the in-laws.'" This is also the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: they are the servants.

Mujahid and Abu Malik al-Ansari said: they are the helpers. This is the narration of Abu Hamzah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Whoever helps you is your hafad."

A poet said:

"The young servants surround them, and they hand over
With their hands the reins of the camels."

'Ata' said: they are the man's children who help him, serve him, support him and attend to him.

Qatadah said: they are the servants, the ones who serve you among your children.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the banun (sons) are the young ones, and the hafadah are the older children who help him in his work.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the children's children.

Ibn Zayd said: they are the sons of the wife from her first husband. This is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the sons of a man's first wife.

Al-'Utbi said: the origin of hafd is racing toward danger and hastening in walking.

So it is said of everyone who hastens in service and work: hafadah, its singular being hafid. From this comes the supplication of the witr prayer: "To You we strive and hasten," meaning we hasten to work in Your obedience.

Ibn Jarir recited [for al-Ra'i]:

"I burdened with its unknown things Yamani she-camels
When the drivers hasten on their backs."

﴿وَرَزَقَكُمْ مِنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ﴾, "and provided you with good things. ﴿أَفَبِالْبَاطِلِ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾", "Then do they believe in falsehood?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: in idols.

﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, that is, the false monotheism; the devil commanded them to slaughter the baheerah, the saa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham. ﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ﴾, by what Allah made lawful for them, ﴿هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, they deny, they reject its being made lawful.

﴿وَيَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَمْلِكُ لَهُمْ رِزْقًا مِنَ السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾, that is, the rain, ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾, that is, the plants.

﴿شَيْئًا﴾. Al-Akhfash said: it is a substitute for rizq, and it has the meaning: they do not own any provision, a little or a lot. Al-Farra' said: shay'an (anything) is in the accusative because the word rizq is applied to it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [Surat al-Mursalat: 25-26], meaning it gathers the living and the dead. Similarly His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan near of kin﴾ [Surat al-Balad: 14-15].

﴿وَلَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ﴾, "and they are not able", that is, they have no power over anything. ﴿فَلَا تَضْرِبُوا لِلَّهِ الْأَمْثَالَ﴾, "So do not coin parables for Allah", that is, similitudes and likenesses, lest they liken Him to His creation and make a partner for Him, for He is One with no like. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ﴾, "Indeed Allah knows" the error of what they coin of parables for Him, ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, "and you do not know" the correctness of that from its error.

﴿And Allah sends down from the sky water﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and He revives the earth after its death﴾, after its barrenness and its being worn out. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen﴾, with the hearing of the hearts and not the hearing of the ears.

﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾, an admonition. ﴿We give you to drink﴾.

The people of Medina, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and 'Asim read ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ﴾ with a fatha on the nun (nasqikum).

It is related from al-Kisa'i that the Arabs say أسقيته نهرا (asqaytuhu nahran, "I gave him a river to water him") and أسقيته لبنا (asqaytuhu laban, "I gave him milk") when they mean to provide a continuous supply, but when they mean that they gave him a single drink, they say سقيناه (saqaynahu), without the alif.

Others said: "They are two dialects, and what indicates this is the saying of Labid in describing the watering:

"He gave drink to my people, the Banu Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilal."

He combined the two dialects.

"When you see the stars of Leo
Rise over its forehead and the khara and the kanad,
And Suhayl sets at al-Fadih, and it becomes spoiled,
And the milk of the she-camels becomes good and cool."

﴿وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ﴾, "And your Lord inspired the bee." That is, He cast [into its ears] or threw into its souls, and it understood it. The nahl (bee) is the wasps of honey, and its singular is nahlah.

﴿أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ﴾, "that take for yourselves houses in the mountains, in the trees, and in what they build". Ibn Zayd said: it means the vineyard.

﴿ثُمَّ كُلِي مِنْ كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ﴾, "Then eat from all the fruits". The meaning of "all" is not generality; it is like His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾, and His saying: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾.

﴿فَاسْلُكِي سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًا﴾, "So follow the ways of your Lord, submissively." That is, enter the paths of your Lord.

Some said: al-dhulul means the paths, and it is said they are made easy for the bees. Mujahid said: "No place is difficult for them that they have traveled."

Others said: al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees [in Tafsir al-Tabari (14/184): it is an attribute of the paths, attributed to Mujahid, then he mentioned the view that al-dhulul is an attribute of the bees, and he preferred the first].

Qatadah and others said: it means obedient and submissive.

﴿يَخْرُجُ مِنْ بُطُونِهَا شَرَابٌ مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ﴾, "From their bellies comes a drink of varying colours", white, red and yellow, ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾, "in it is healing for mankind."

It is related that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My brother has a pain in his stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." He went and came back and said: "I gave him to drink, and it did not help him at all." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Go and give him honey to drink, for Allah has spoken the truth and his brother's stomach has lied." [7] [Sahih Muslim, 7/26, and Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3/276.] So he gave him to drink, and it was as if he had been released from a fetter. [It was related by] 'Atiyyah from Abu al-Mutawakkil from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Mujahid said: ﴿فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ means in the Qur'an. The first view is more correct and better suited to the apparent sense of the Book.

Waki' related from Sufyan from Abu Ishaq from Abu al-Ahwas from 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), who said: honey is a healing from every disease, and the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts.

Al-A'mash from Khaytham from al-Aswad said: 'Abd Allah said: "Keep to the two healings: honey and the Qur'an."

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾, that is, in what we have mentioned, ﴿لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ﴾, "a sign for a people who reflect", so that they may take lesson.

﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ ثُمَّ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ﴾, "And Allah created you, then He takes you back", as children, youths and elders. ﴿وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرَدُّ إِلَى أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ﴾, "And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age", that is, its worst. It is said from this: "the man became base and despicable (dhall al-rajul wa-fasal, yarthul rudhalah wa-rudhulah, wa-radhalthuhu ana)" [Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/186].

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means to the lowest of life.

Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: it means senility.

Qatadah said: the most abject age is seventy years.

Al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: the most abject age is seventy-five years.

﴿لِكَيْ لَا يَعْلَمَ بَعْدَ عِلْمٍ شَيْئًا﴾, "so that he knows nothing after knowing", that is, he does not reason after his first reason at all.

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ قَدِيرٌ﴾, "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful." Its parallel is in Surat al-Hajj [Surat al-Hajj: 5].

﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ فِي الرِّزْقِ﴾, "And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. So those who have been favoured in provision will not give their provision ﴿عَلَى مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ﴾, "to what their right hands possess", of the slaves, so that they and their slaves would be equal in that." Allah, may His praise be exalted, says: they do not accept that they and their slaves be equal in what We have provided them, yet they have made My servants partners in My dominion and My authority. This parable is used to establish the proof against the polytheists. This is a parable which Allah, mighty and majestic, has coined: none of you shares his slave's wife, his relatives or his wealth with him. Will you then equate with Allah His creation and His servants? If you do not accept this for yourselves, then Allah is more worthy to be exalted above it, and do not equate any of His servants or creatures with Him [see Tafsir al-Tabari, 14/188].

'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: this verse was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran when they said: "Jesus is the son of God." It says: the master does not give back from what his right hand possesses from what He has provided, until the master and the owned are equal in the means of livelihood. How then do you accept for Me what you do not accept for yourselves? Its parallel is in Surat al-Rum: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [Surat al-Rum: 28] [a parable you witness].

He said: ﴿أَفَبِنِعْمَةِ اللَّهِ يَجْحَدُونَ﴾, "Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?" by associating others with Him.

'Asim read with the ta' (tajhadun, in the second person), because of His saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ﴾ and ﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ﴾.

The rest read with the ya' (yajhadun, in the third person), because of His saying: ﴿فَهُمْ فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ﴾ [Surat al-Nahl: 71], and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because the reported party is closer to it.

﴿وَاللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا﴾, "And Allah made for you spouses from yourselves", meaning that He created from Adam his wife Hawwa'. ﴿وَجَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَزْوَاجِكُمْ بَنِينَ وَحَفَدَةً﴾, "and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren."

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Ad'ha said: the hafadah are the in-laws, the husband's sons-in-law (who are married to his daughters).

Shu'bah related from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, who said: I heard Zirr ibn Hubaysh, a foreigner who had lived through the Jahiliyyah, say: "I used to hold the Mushaf for 'Abd Allah, and he came to this verse, and he asked: 'Do you know what al-hafadah are?' I said: 'They are a man's entourage.' 'Abd Allah said: 'No, but they are the in-laws.'" This is also the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: they are the servants.

Mujahid and Abu Malik al-Ansari said: they are the helpers. This is the narration of Abu Hamzah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Whoever helps you is your hafad."

A poet said:

"The young servants surround them, and they hand over
With their hands the reins of the camels."

'Ata' said: they are the man's children who help him, serve him, support him and attend to him.

Qatadah said: they are the servants, the ones who serve you among your children.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the banun (sons) are the young ones, and the hafadah are the older children who help him in his work.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the children's children.

Ibn Zayd said: they are the sons of the wife from her first husband. This is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the sons of a man's first wife.

Al-'Utbi said: the origin of hafd is racing toward danger and hastening in walking.

So it is said of everyone who hastens in service and work: hafadah, its singular being hafid. From this comes the supplication of the witr prayer: "To You we strive and hasten," meaning we hasten to work in Your obedience.

Ibn Jarir recited [for al-Ra'i]:

"I burdened with its unknown things Yamani she-camels
When the drivers hasten on their backs."

﴿وَرَزَقَكُمْ مِنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ﴾, "and provided you with good things. ﴿أَفَبِالْبَاطِلِ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾", "Then do they believe in falsehood?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: in idols.

﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, that is, the false monotheism; the devil commanded them to slaughter the baheerah, the saa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham. ﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ﴾, by what Allah made lawful for them, ﴿هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, they deny, they reject its being made lawful.

﴿وَيَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَمْلِكُ لَهُمْ رِزْقًا مِنَ السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾, that is, the rain, ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾, that is, the plants.

﴿شَيْئًا﴾. Al-Akhfash said: it is a substitute for rizq, and it has the meaning: they do not own any provision, a little or a lot. Al-Farra' said: shay'an (anything) is in the accusative because the word rizq is applied to it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [Surat al-Mursalat: 25-26], meaning it gathers the living and the dead. Similarly His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan near of kin﴾ [Surat al-Balad: 14-15].

﴿وَلَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ﴾, "and they are not able", that is, they have no power over anything. ﴿فَلَا تَضْرِبُوا لِلَّهِ الْأَمْثَالَ﴾, "So do not coin parables for Allah", that is, similitudes and likenesses, lest they liken Him to His creation and make a partner for Him, for He is One with no like. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ﴾, "Indeed Allah knows" the error of what they coin of parables for Him, ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, "and you do not know" the correctness of that from its error.

﴿And Allah sends down from the sky water﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and He revives the earth after its death﴾, after its barrenness and its being worn out. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen﴾, with the hearing of the hearts and not the hearing of the ears.

﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾, an admonition. ﴿We give you to drink﴾.

The people of Medina, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and 'Asim read ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ﴾ with a fatha on the nun (nasqikum).

The rest read it with a damma on the nun (nusqikum), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, saying: "Because it is a drink that is continuous."

It is related from al-Kisa'i that the Arabs say أسقيته نهرا (asqaytuhu nahran, "I gave him a river to water him") and أسقيته لبنا (asqaytuhu laban, "I gave him milk") when they mean to provide a continuous supply, but when they mean that they gave him a single drink, they say سقيناه (saqaynahu), without the alif.

Others said: "They are two dialects, and what indicates this is the saying of Labid in describing the watering:

"He gave drink to my people, the Banu Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilal."

He combined the two dialects.

﴿مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "from what is in their bellies", and he did not say بطونها (butuniha), although الأنعام (al-an'am, the livestock) is a plural. Al-Mubarrad said: the pronoun refers to النعم (al-ni'am, "the cattle"), and النعم and الأنعام are one and the same, and the word النعم is used. He cited in evidence a rajaz verse of one of the Bedouin:

"When you see the stars of Leo
Rise over its forehead and the khara and the kanad,
And Suhayl sets at al-Fadih, and it becomes spoiled,
And the milk of the she-camels becomes good and cool."

He did not say فبردت (fabaradat), because he referred it back to اللبن (al-laban, "the milk") or الخراة (al-kharah). [Thus in the original.]

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: نعم (ni'am, "cattle") is masculine and feminine. Whoever makes it feminine does so for the sense of plurality, and whoever makes it masculine does so for the form of the word, and because it has no singular from its own form.

A poet said about it:

"Every year there are cattle that you keep,
A people impregnate them and you deliver them,
Indeed they have palm trees, so they do not protect them."

Al-Kisa'i said: the pronoun refers back to what is intended, in the bellies of what has been mentioned.

Some of them said: he meant the bellies of this thing, like Allah's saying: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord"﴾, and His saying: ﴿"And indeed I am sending a gift to them"﴾ up to ﴿So when he came to Solomon﴾, and He did not say "she came."

Al-Salt al-'Abdi said:

"Indeed, generosity and manliness have enclosed
A grave in Marw, on the clear road."

Another said:

"And 'Afra' is the nearest of people to me in affection,
And 'Afra' is far from me, the one who turns away and holds back."

Another said:

"When people are people and the lands are in prosperity,
And the mother of 'Ammar is a friend who helps."

All of that is according to the meaning of this person and this thing.

Al-Mu'arrij said: the pronoun refers back to the part and the portion, as if He said: ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ﴾, "We give you to drink from what is in their bellies," which is the milk, since not all of them have milk, but only those that have milk are watered, so the milk is implied in it.

﴿مِنْ بَيْنِ فَرْثٍ﴾, "from between dung", which is what is in the paunch; when it leaves it, it is no longer called فرث (farth). ﴿وَدَمٍ﴾, "and blood", ﴿لَبَنًا خَالِصًا﴾, "pure milk", purified from the dung and the blood and not mixed with them, ﴿سَائِغًا لِلشَّارِبِينَ﴾, "palatable to the drinkers", ready, pleasant, sliding down the throat without choking its drinker. It was said: no one has ever choked on milk.

Ibn 'Abbas said: when the animal eats the fodder and it settles in its paunch at that time, its lowest part is dung, its middle is milk, and its uppermost part is the blood of the liver. [So what was] of these three kinds is divided: the blood flows in the veins, the milk flows into the udder, and the dung remains as it is.

﴿وَمِنْ ثَمَرَاتِ النَّخِيلِ وَالْأَعْنَابِ﴾, meaning: this too is a lesson, in what We give you to drink and provide you with, from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes, ﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنْهُ﴾, "you take from it". The pronoun in His saying ﴿مِنْهُ﴾ refers back to those mentioned.

﴿سَكَرًا وَرِزْقًا حَسَنًا﴾, "intoxicant and good provision".

Some people said: al-sakar is wine, and al-rizq al-hasan is vinegar, grapes, dates and raisins. They said: this is the view on the prohibition of wine, and this view was held by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Amr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ayyub, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla and al-Kalbi. It is the narration of 'Amr ibn Sufyan al-Basri from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-sakar is what is forbidden of its fruit, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is lawful of its fruit.

As for al-sakar, it is the intoxicants of these foreigners, and as for al-rizq al-hasan, it is what you soak, what you make vinegar from, and what you eat.

He said: this verse was revealed when wine had not yet been forbidden, and its prohibition was revealed after that in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Al-Sha'bi said: al-sakar is what is drunk, and al-rizq al-hasan is what is eaten.

Al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas that the Abyssinians call vinegar al-sakar.

Others said: al-sakar is intoxicating nabidh, which is the steeped infusion of dates and raisins when it has fermented, and the boiled-down juice. This is the view of al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi, according to the narration of Mujalid, and Abu Rawq, and the view of al-Nakha'i, and the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: it is date nabidh.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Wine is what is made from grapes, sakar is from dates, bit' is from honey, mizr is from maize, [and al-bira] [as in the manuscript, though it is not found in the source] from wheat, and I forbid you from every intoxicant." [6] [Musnad Abi Ya'la, 13/216, with variation.]

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-sakar means taste; it is said: "This is sakar for you," meaning a taste for you.

He recited:

"I made the faults of the noble ones a taste."

It says: the master does not give back from what his right hand possesses from what He has provided, until the master and the owned are equal in the means of livelihood. How then do you accept for Me what you do not accept for yourselves? Its parallel is in Surat al-Rum: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [Surat al-Rum: 28] [a parable you witness].

He said: ﴿أَفَبِنِعْمَةِ اللَّهِ يَجْحَدُونَ﴾, "Then do they deny the blessing of Allah?" by associating others with Him.

'Asim read with the ta' (tajhadun, in the second person), because of His saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ﴾ and ﴿وَاللَّهُ فَضَّلَ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ﴾.

The rest read with the ya' (yajhadun, in the third person), because of His saying: ﴿فَهُمْ فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ﴾ [Surat al-Nahl: 71], and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because the reported party is closer to it.

﴿وَاللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا﴾, "And Allah made for you spouses from yourselves", meaning that He created from Adam his wife Hawwa'. ﴿وَجَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَزْوَاجِكُمْ بَنِينَ وَحَفَدَةً﴾, "and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren."

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Ad'ha said: the hafadah are the in-laws, the husband's sons-in-law (who are married to his daughters).

Shu'bah related from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, who said: I heard Zirr ibn Hubaysh, a foreigner who had lived through the Jahiliyyah, say: "I used to hold the Mushaf for 'Abd Allah, and he came to this verse, and he asked: 'Do you know what al-hafadah are?' I said: 'They are a man's entourage.' 'Abd Allah said: 'No, but they are the in-laws.'" This is also the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: they are the servants.

Mujahid and Abu Malik al-Ansari said: they are the helpers. This is the narration of Abu Hamzah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Whoever helps you is your hafad."

A poet said:

"The young servants surround them, and they hand over
With their hands the reins of the camels."

'Ata' said: they are the man's children who help him, serve him, support him and attend to him.

Qatadah said: they are the servants, the ones who serve you among your children.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: the banun (sons) are the young ones, and the hafadah are the older children who help him in his work.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the children's children.

Ibn Zayd said: they are the sons of the wife from her first husband. This is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the sons of a man's first wife.

Al-'Utbi said: the origin of hafd is racing toward danger and hastening in walking.

So it is said of everyone who hastens in service and work: hafadah, its singular being hafid. From this comes the supplication of the witr prayer: "To You we strive and hasten," meaning we hasten to work in Your obedience.

Ibn Jarir recited [for al-Ra'i]:

"I burdened with its unknown things Yamani she-camels
When the drivers hasten on their backs."

﴿وَرَزَقَكُمْ مِنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ﴾, "and provided you with good things. ﴿أَفَبِالْبَاطِلِ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾", "Then do they believe in falsehood?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: in idols.

﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, that is, the false monotheism; the devil commanded them to slaughter the baheerah, the saa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham. ﴿وَبِنِعْمَتِ اللَّهِ﴾, by what Allah made lawful for them, ﴿هُمْ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾, they deny, they reject its being made lawful.

﴿وَيَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَمْلِكُ لَهُمْ رِزْقًا مِنَ السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾, that is, the rain, ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ﴾, that is, the plants.

﴿شَيْئًا﴾. Al-Akhfash said: it is a substitute for rizq, and it has the meaning: they do not own any provision, a little or a lot. Al-Farra' said: shay'an (anything) is in the accusative because the word rizq is applied to it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [Surat al-Mursalat: 25-26], meaning it gathers the living and the dead. Similarly His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan near of kin﴾ [Surat al-Balad: 14-15].

﴿وَلَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ﴾, "and they are not able", that is, they have no power over anything. ﴿فَلَا تَضْرِبُوا لِلَّهِ الْأَمْثَالَ﴾, "So do not coin parables for Allah", that is, similitudes and likenesses, lest they liken Him to His creation and make a partner for Him, for He is One with no like. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ﴾, "Indeed Allah knows" the error of what they coin of parables for Him, ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, "and you do not know" the correctness of that from its error.

Then God struck a parable of the believer and the disbeliever, and He, mighty is His majesty, said: "God strikes a parable: a slave owned, who has power over nothing" (Qur'an 16:75). This is the likeness of the disbeliever, whom God gave wealth, yet he did not send forward any good and did not act with it in obedience to God, the Exalted. "And one whom We have provided with goodly provision from Us, so he spends from it secretly and openly" (16:75). This is the likeness of the believer, whom God gave wealth; he acted with it in obedience to God and spent it in what pleases God, secretly and openly, so God rewarded him with lasting bliss in Paradise. "Are they equal?" (16:75). He did not say "are they two equal" (yastawiyan) because of (man), since it is an indefinite noun that can be used for the singular, the dual, the plural, the feminine and the masculine. Likewise is His saying: "And they worship besides God that which possesses for them no provision" (16:73), then He said: "And they are not able" (16:73), using the plural because of (ma). The meaning of the verse: are this poverty and stinginess and this wealth and generosity equal? Likewise, the disbelieving rebel who opposes God's command and the believer who obeys Him are not equal.

Ibn Jurayj narrated from 'Ata': "a slave owned" (16:75) — he said: this is Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. "And one whom We have provided with goodly provision from Us" (16:75) — Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him).

Then He said: "Praise be to God. But most of them do not know" (16:75). God, the Exalted, says: The matter is not as they do, nor is the saying as they say. The idols have no hand in it, and no favour for which they should be praised. Rather, praise belongs entirely and purely to God, because He is the Bestower of blessing, the Creator and the Provider. But most of these disbelievers do not know that it is so. Then He struck another parable concerning Himself and the idols: "And God strikes a parable of two men: one of them dumb, who has power over nothing, and he is a burden upon his master; wherever he directs him, he brings no good" (16:76). "Wherever he directs him" means he sends him, and "brings no good" because he does not understand what is said, nor does he understand from him.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "Wherever he directs him, he brings no good" — this is a parable for the idol, which does not hear, does not speak, does not understand and does not act, and is a burden upon its keeper, who needs to carry it, set it down and serve it. "Is he equal to one who commands justice" (16:76), meaning God, who is capable and speaks, commanding the command of monotheism. He is not like your idol, which does not command monotheism, "while he is upon a straight path" (16:76).

Al-Kalbi said: that is, "while he is guiding you to a straight path." It was also said: he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "while he is upon a straight path" (16:76).

Al-Kalbi said: that is, "while he is guiding you to a straight path" (16:76).

Another opinion: whoever says that all Muslims, both believer and disbeliever, is meant; this is the narration of 'Uqbah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibrahim ibn 'Ikrimah ibn Ya'la ibn Munabbih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: this verse was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) and his freedman. Muqatil said: this verse was revealed concerning Hashim ibn 'Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Rabi'ah al-Qurashi, who was a man of little good who opposed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

'Ata' said: [the dumb man is Ubayy ibn Khalaf]. "And one who commands justice" (16:76) refers to Hamzah, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and 'Uthman ibn Maz'un.

"And to God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye" (16:77), meaning in its nearness of occurrence and swiftness of its establishment, "or it is nearer" (16:77). Rather, it is nearer. "Indeed, God is over all things competent" (16:77). It was revealed concerning the disbelievers who asked for the Hour to be hastened, mocking.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 16, verses 79–83:

Ye have not seen (﴿أَلَمْ يَرَوْا﴾). Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamzah and Ya'qub read it with the ta' (as ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَوْا﴾, "Have you not seen").

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: serpents like Bactrian camels and scorpions like mules, each of whose sting causes its victim to feel its burning for forty years.

It is also said: they will pass from the heat of the Fire to the Zamharīr (extreme cold), and then, from the severity of the cold, they will hasten back to the Fire.

It is said also: [the increase is that] they will bear the burdens of their followers, as God, exalted is He, says: "And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens" [Surah al-ʿAnkabūt: 13].

It is also said: the punishment will be doubled for them.

[They will be punished] for what they used to corrupt in the world, namely disbelief and barring people from faith.

And on the Day We raise up in every nation a witness against them from among themselves, meaning against them; and He said "from among themselves" because He used to send to each nation prophets from among them. And We have brought you, O Muhammad, as a witness over these to whom you were sent. And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation (tibyān) for everything that is needed, of commands and prohibitions, of the lawful and the unlawful, of the prescribed punishments and rulings, and as guidance, mercy, and good tidings for the Muslims.

On the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness, [namely] their messenger, then it will not be permitted to those who disbelieved [to offer excuses], nor will they be asked to make amends (yustaʿtabūn), that is, they will not be required to win the pleasure of their Lord, because the Hereafter is not an abode of obligation; nor will they be given the chance to return to the worldly abode [so that they might repent]. And when those who did wrong see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved (yunẓarūn), that is, delayed. And when those who associated partners [with God] see on the Day of Resurrection their partners, that is, their idols, they will say: "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You," [as lords] and worship them. But they will throw at them the word, that is, they will say to them, as in the expression "alqaytu ilayka kadhā" (I conveyed to you such-and-such), meaning: "You are indeed liars," [in calling us gods], for we did not call you to our worship, nor did we know that you were worshipping us. And they will offer submission (al-salam) to God on that Day, that is, the polytheists will submit and yield to His judgment concerning them, and their gods will not avail them at all, and what they used to fabricate, [claiming] that they would intercede for them, will be lost to them (ḍalla, meaning zāla), [......] [[unreadable text.]] from them.

Those who disbelieved and barred [others] from the way of God—We shall increase them in punishment upon punishment.

﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice﴾, meaning fairness, ﴿and beneficence﴾ toward people. Al-Walibi related from Ibn 'Abbas: "Justice" is tawhid (affirming God's oneness), and "beneficence" is performing the obligatory duties.

[It has also been said:] "Justice" is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and "beneficence" is sincerity in it.

'Ata' related from him: "Justice" is the affirmation of the equals (al-Anadad) [i.e., denying God any equals], and "beneficence" is that you worship Allah as if you see Him. Muqatil said: "Justice" is tawhid, and "beneficence" is pardoning people.

It has also been said: justice is in actions and beneficence is in words. This is like His saying: ﴿And speak to people good words﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:83].

﴿And giving to kinsfolk﴾ means maintaining the ties of kinship. ﴿And He forbids what is shameful﴾, meaning the ugly deeds and words.

Ibn 'Abbas said: [the shameful is] fornication.

﴿And the blameworthy﴾ is what is not recognized in the Law (shari'ah) or the Sunnah. ﴿And oppression﴾ is wickedness and injustice.

Ibn 'Uyayna said: justice is [maintained in] the secret and the public. Beneficence is that one's inner state is better than one's outward conduct. The shameful is that one's outward conduct is better than one's inner state.

﴿He admonishes you that you may be mindful﴾, meaning that you may take admonition.

Qatadah said: Allah the Exalted commanded His servants to noble character and its highest forms, and forbade them from its base and lowly forms.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "The most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an is this verse."

Shahr ibn Hawshab related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting in the courtyard of his house in Makkah, 'Uthman ibn Maz'un passed by him and greeted the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger said to him: "Will you not sit?" He said: "Yes," and sat facing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. While he was speaking with him, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ raised his gaze to the sky and looked for a while. Then he began lowering his gaze until it fell on the ground to his right. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned away from his companion 'Uthman toward where he had lowered his gaze, and began nodding his head as if he were understanding something being said to him. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ raised his gaze to the sky as he had done the first time, and followed it until it disappeared into the sky. Then he turned to 'Uthman in his former state. 'Uthman said: "O Muhammad, in all the time I have sat with you, I have never seen you do what you did this morning." He said: "And what did you see me do?" He said: "I saw you raise your gaze to the sky, then lower it to your right, and you turned toward it and left me, and you began nodding your head as if you were understanding something said to you." He said: "Did you notice that?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Jibril came to me just now while you were sitting here." He said: "Yes. What did he say to you?" He said: "He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and beneficence﴾ to the end of the verse."

'Uthman said: "At that moment faith settled in my heart, and I loved Muhammad ﷺ."

Hammad ibn Zayd related from Ayyub from 'Ikrimah from the Prophet ﷺ that he recited to al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice﴾ up to the end of the verse. [Al-Walid] said: "O nephew, repeat it." He repeated it to him. He said: "By Allah, it has a sweetness, and it has a brilliance. Its upper part bears fruit and its lower part is abundant. It is not the speech of a human being." Then he did not accept Islam, so Allah revealed concerning him: ﴿And he gave a little and withheld﴾ [An-Najm 53:34].

﴿And fulfill the covenant of Allah when you have made a covenant﴾ and ﴿do not break oaths after their confirmation﴾, meaning their strengthening [and not breaking them]. "Tawkid" (confirmation) is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz; as for the people of Najd, they say: "akkadtu ta'kidan" (I confirmed a confirmation). ﴿And you have made Allah your surety﴾ for fulfillment. ﴿Indeed, Allah knows what you do.⁠﴾ The scholars differed about who this verse was revealed concerning, although its ruling is general.

Some of them said: it was revealed concerning those who pledged allegiance (bay'ah) to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Allah commanded them to fulfill it.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning the alliances of the people of Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance).

Then He, may His praise be exalted, gave an example of breaking a covenant, saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And do not be like one who unravels her yarn after it has been made strong﴾, meaning after its twisting and firm binding. Some linguists said: "al-quwwah" (strength) is what is spun on a single strand and not doubled.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: she was a foolish, senseless woman from Quraysh called Rita bint 'Amr ibn Sa'd ibn Ka'b ibn Zayd Manat ibn Tamim. She had taken a spindle of about the length of a forearm, and a whorl like a finger, and she twisted a bone according to its size. She used to spin wool, hair, and fur, and she would order her maidservants to do the same. They would spin from morning until midday. When midday came, she would order her maidservants to unravel everything they had spun. This was her habit.

[The verse says] ﴿into fragments﴾, meaning unravelled pieces; its singular is "nakthah," which is anything unravelled after being twisted, whether yarn or ropes.

﴿Taking your oaths as deception between you﴾, meaning deceit, treachery, and trickery.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: every matter that is not sound is "dakhal" (deceit).

﴿That one community may be greater⁠﴾ meaning, so that a community may be ﴿more numerous⁠﴾, more abundant and more honored, than another community.

Mujahid said: that was because they used to make alliances, then they found a group greater than them and mightier, and they became certain of them, so these swore to them and made alliances with the more numerous. So Allah the Exalted forbade them from that.

﴿Indeed, Allah only tests you by it﴾, meaning He tries you through His command to you to fulfill the covenant. ﴿And He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that over which you used to differ⁠﴾ in the world. ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one community⁠﴾, upon one religion. ﴿But He leads astray whom He wills⁠﴾ by abandoning them, as an act of justice from Him toward them, ﴿and guides whom He wills⁠﴾ by granting them success, as an act of grace from Him. ﴿And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do.⁠﴾

﴿And do not take your oaths as deception⁠﴾, meaning deceit and corruption, ﴿between you⁠﴾, by which you deceive people, so that you rest in your oaths while they feel secure, and then you break them and disagree about them. ﴿Lest a foot slip after being firmly planted⁠﴾, meaning that you be destroyed after having been secure. The Arabs say of everyone who is afflicted after well-being, or who falls into a calamity after safety: "his feet slipped."

Like the words of the poet:

"He will prevent you from winning the race if you were a winner, and you will be struck if both your feet slip."

﴿And taste the evil⁠﴾, meaning the punishment, ﴿for what you have hindered from the way of Allah. And for you is a great punishment.⁠﴾

﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price⁠﴾, meaning do not break your covenants seeking in breaking them a small worldly gain in exchange. Rather, fulfill them, for what is with Allah of reward for you for fulfilling that is ﴿better for you, if you only knew⁠﴾. He distinguishes between the two exchanged items, then explains: ﴿What is with you will end, and what is with Allah remains.⁠﴾ ﴿And We will surely reward⁠﴾ is with the nun (we) by 'Asim; the others read it with the ya' (he).

﴿Those who were patient⁠﴾ in fulfillment, in ease and in hardship, ﴿We will give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do⁠﴾, not the worst of it, and will forgive their misdeeds by His grace. ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life⁠﴾. The scholars differed about it:

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', and al-Dahhak said: it is lawful provision. This is the narration of Ibn Abi Malik and Abu al-Rabi' from Ibn 'Abbas.

al-Hasan, 'Ali, Zayd, and Wahb ibn Munabbih said: it is contentment and satisfaction with what Allah has decreed. This is the narration of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: it means excelling in obedience. This is the narration of 'Ubayd ibn Sulaym from al-Dahhak, who said: "Whoever does righteousness while he is a believer, in poverty or in ease, has a good life. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of Allah, does not believe, and does no righteous deed, has a constricted life with no good in it."

Abu Bakr al-Warraq: it is the sweetness of obedience.

al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas: it is happiness. Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd: it is Paradise. Similarly it was related from al-Hasan, who said: "Life is not made good for anyone except in Paradise."

﴿And We will surely reward them their reward according to the best of what they used to do.⁠﴾

Abu Salih said: some people from among the People of the Torah, the People of the Gospel, and the idol-worshippers sat together. The first group said: "We are better." The second said: "We are better." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge with Allah from Satan, the accursed⁠﴾, meaning: when you are reciting the Qur'an, seek refuge.

Muhammad ibn Jarir said, and others said: its meaning is: when you intend to recite the Qur'an, seek refuge. Like His saying: ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces⁠﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 5:6], meaning purification precedes prayer; and His saying: ﴿When you divorce women, divorce them for their waiting period⁠﴾ [At-Talaq 65:1], meaning when you intend to divorce women, because it is impossible that He commands them to a specific divorce after the divorce has already passed.

As for the ruling of the verse: know that seeking refuge when reciting the Qur'an is recommended, in prayer and outside prayer. This is the view of the majority of jurists, except Malik, who says one seeks refuge only in the night prayers of Ramadan. He argued with what was narrated: that the Prophet ﷺ used to open the prayer with ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds⁠﴾.

The interpretation of this hadith is that he used to begin the recitation in the prayer with ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds⁠﴾. What supports this is that the prayer opens with the takbir without disagreement, so the apparent meaning of the report is set aside.

What supports our position is the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im, who said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ praying, and he said: 'Allah is greatest, greatly; and praise be to Allah abundantly, and glory be to Allah morning and evening. I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed: from his breath, his spittle, and his pricking.'"

Ibn Mas'ud said: "Its breath is pride, its spittle is poetry, and its pricking is sickness," meaning madness. Once this is established, it is confirmed that the earlier report is set aside in its apparent meaning and taken in its intended sense.

The jurists differed about the time of seeking refuge. Most of them said: before recitation. This is the view of the majority and is the correct and well-known position.

Abu Hurayrah said: one seeks refuge after recitation, and Dawud ibn 'Ali held this view.

Malik said, regarding the prayer in which one seeks refuge, which is the night prayer of Ramadan: one seeks refuge after recitation, and he argued from the apparent meaning of the verse. We have explained its meaning. The evidence that it is before recitation is what Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: 'I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed,' and then he would recite."

As for the discussion of the place of seeking refuge in prayer, al-Shafi'i said: one says it at the beginning of the first rak'ah. It was also said: if one says it wherever one begins each rak'ah before recitation, that is good, and one may recite it in any part of the prayer, as he was commanded to at the beginning of the first rak'ah. This is the view of most jurists.

Ibn Sirin said: one seeks refuge in every rak'ah before recitation. The correct position is the first, because what is related in the reports is that the Prophet ﷺ only sought refuge in the first rak'ah.

As for its manner in prayer: one looks. If it is a prayer in which the recitation is silent, one makes the seeking refuge silent; and if it is a prayer in which the recitation is aloud:

al-Shafi'i said in al-Umm: it is related that Abu Hurayrah led the people in prayer, raising his voice: "Our Lord, we seek refuge in You from the accursed Satan." And Ibn 'Umar would seek refuge silently.

al-Shafi'i said: if one wishes, one says it aloud, and if one wishes, one says it silently.

al-Tha'labi said: the preferred option is silence, to distinguish between what is Qur'an and what is not Qur'an.

As for the wording of the seeking refuge, the preferable and recommended wording is: "I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed," because of the explicit text of the Qur'an and the continuous chain of narration (al-khabar al-muttasil al-mutasalsil). It is this: I recited to Shaykh Abu al-Fadl Muhammad ibn Abi Ja'far al-Khuza'i, and I said: "I seek refuge with the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." He said to me: "Say: 'I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan,' in all places." I then recited to Abu al-Husayn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad in Basra, and I said: "I seek refuge with the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," and he said: "Say: 'I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan.'" I then recited to 'Abd Allah Abu Hamid al-Zanjani, and I said: "I seek refuge with the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan," and he said to me: "Say: 'I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan.'" I then recited to Abu 'Uthman Isma'il ibn Ibrahim al-Ahwazi, and I said: "I seek refuge with the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan," and he said to me: "Say: 'I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan.'" I then recited to Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Bistam, and I said: "I seek refuge with the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," and he said to me: "Say: 'I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan.'" I then recited to Rawh ibn 'Abd al-Mu'min, and I said: "I seek refuge with the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," and he said to me: "Say: 'I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan.'" I then recited to Ya'qub al-Hadrami, and I said: "I seek refuge with the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," and he said to me: "Say: 'I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan.'" The jurists differed about the time of seeking refuge. Most of them said: before recitation. This is the view of the majority and is the correct and well-known position.

Malik said, regarding the prayer in which one seeks refuge, which is the night prayer of Ramadan: one seeks refuge after recitation, and he argued from the apparent meaning of the verse. We have explained its meaning. It was also said: if one says it wherever one begins each rak'ah before recitation, that is good, and one may recite it in any part of the prayer, as he was commanded to at the beginning of the first rak'ah. This is the view of most jurists.

Ibn Sirin said: one seeks refuge in every rak'ah before recitation. The correct position is the first, because what is related in the reports is that the Prophet ﷺ only sought refuge in the first rak'ah.

As for its manner in prayer: one looks. If it is a prayer in which the recitation is silent, one makes the seeking refuge silent; and if it is a prayer in which the recitation is aloud:

Malik said, regarding the prayer in which one seeks refuge, which is the night prayer of Ramadan: one seeks refuge after recitation, and he argued from the apparent meaning of the verse. We have explained its meaning. It was also said: if one says it wherever one begins each rak'ah before recitation, that is good, and one may recite it in any part of the prayer, as he was commanded to at the beginning of the first rak'ah. This is the view of most jurists.

Ibn Sirin said: one seeks refuge in every rak'ah before recitation. The correct position is the first, because what is related in the reports is that the Prophet ﷺ only sought refuge in the first rak'ah.

As for its manner in prayer: one looks. If it is a prayer in which the recitation is silent, one makes the seeking refuge silent; and if it is a prayer in which the recitation is aloud:

He said: "Did you notice that?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Jibril came to me just now while you were sitting here." He said: "Yes. What did he say to you?" He said: "He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and beneficence﴾ to the end of the verse."

'Uthman said: "At that moment faith settled in my heart, and I loved Muhammad ﷺ."

Hammad ibn Zayd related from Ayyub from 'Ikrimah from the Prophet ﷺ that he recited to al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice﴾ up to the end of the verse. [Al-Walid] said: "O nephew, repeat it." He repeated it to him. He said: "By Allah, it has a sweetness, and it has a brilliance. Its upper part bears fruit and its lower part is abundant. Mujahid and Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning the alliances of the people of Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance).

Some linguists said: "al-quwwah" (strength) is what is spun on a single strand and not doubled.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: she was a foolish, senseless woman from Quraysh called Rita bint 'Amr ibn Sa'd ibn Ka'b ibn Zayd Manat ibn Tamim. She had taken a spindle of about the length of a forearm, and a whorl like a finger, and she twisted a bone according to its size. The jurists agreed that one compelled to disbelieve, or to insult the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Companions, or to abandon prayer, or to slander a chaste woman, or similar things of abandoning obedience and committing doubtful acts, under a threat that destroys or severe beating that he cannot bear, may do what he is compelled to do. I said: "O Messenger of Allah, does a believer steal?" He said: "That may happen." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, does a believer lie?" He said: "No, Allah said, ﴿Only those fabricate falsehood who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾" [al-Da'awat lil-Rawandi: 118, no. 275].

These are two clauses; if they combine, one of them depends on the other, so their answer is one, like the saying of the speaker: "Whoever comes to us, whoever is good, we will honor him," meaning: whoever among those who come to us is good, we will honor him [see Tafsir al-Tabari: 14/236].

Mujahid said: This verse was revealed about some people of Mecca who believed. They set out seeking Medina, but the Quraysh overtook them on the road and tempted them, and they disbelieved under compulsion.

He had come as an emigrant and was dutiful to his mother. She swore that she would not eat bread or sit in shade until her son returned to her. He said: Abu Jahl, who was his maternal half-brother, and another man came to him, and he wanted to return with them. Abu Jahl said to him: "If your mother were hungry, she would not eat; and if she were exposed to the sun, she would not seek shade." Her son said: "Yes, I will go to her and then return." He said: "If you go, do not give your camel to anyone, for you will always have half of your affair as long as you do not give your camel to anyone." So he and Abu Jahl and the man set out. When they were on part of the road, Abu Jahl said: "Let each of us ride the other's camel." So each of them rode the other's camel, and they continued on.

The ruling of the verse:

The jurists agreed that one compelled to disbelieve, or to insult the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Companions, or to abandon prayer, or to slander a chaste woman, or similar things of abandoning obedience and committing doubtful acts, under a threat that destroys or severe beating that he cannot bear, may do what he is compelled to do.
